place/aksum.title: Aksum
place/aksum.summary: Aksum is a town in the Tigray region of northern Ethiopia that was the capital of the Kingdom of Aksum, a trading state active from about the 1st century CE to the 7th century and later, known for its stone stelae, coinage and early adoption of Christianity.
facts: Aksum lies in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, and the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a Greek trade guide of about the 1st century CE, mentions Aksum and its port Adulis on the Red Sea.

Aksumite rulers minted gold, silver and bronze coins from about the late 3rd century CE, and King Ezana adopted Christianity at a date placed variously between about 325 and 340 CE; coins struck afterward bear the cross.
Ezana's inscriptions were written in Ge'ez, Sabaean and Greek.

Aksum's monolithic stelae mark burial sites; the largest, about 33 meters high, fell and broke, and a 24-meter stele taken to Rome by Italian forces in 1937 was returned in 2005 and re-erected in 2008.
Ethiopian Christian tradition holds that the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion at Aksum houses the Ark of the Covenant; the claim cannot be examined.
Aksum declined from the 7th century, and proposed causes include changes in Red Sea trade after the rise of Islam, environmental stress and internal conflict; the causes are debated.
UNESCO inscribed Aksum in 1980.
place/aksum.context: Aksum was the capital of the Kingdom of Aksum, which had contacts with Kingdom of Saba across the Red Sea; its stele was taken during the Second Italo-Ethiopian War's Italian occupation. Later Ethiopian rulers built the Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela. Aksum sits in Classical Antiquity and the region Sub-Saharan Africa, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, Religion and Belief and Art and Ritual.
place/aksum.observer: The Observer notes that Aksum shows a state announcing its meaning-engine through stone and metal: giant stelae over graves, and coins that carried a cross after Ezana's conversion, so that a portable object spread the ruler's story-glue across the trading network. The taking and return of the stele show that monuments become claim-lines of another kind when moved. The Ark tradition is a belief held by a community that cannot be tested, and the Observer records it as belief, neither endorsing nor dismissing it. The reading would weaken if the coin evidence proves too sparse to date Ezana's change of religion.
questions: Why did Aksum decline from the 7th century?
How large was Aksum's population at its height?

place/amazon-river.title: Amazon River
place/amazon-river.summary: The Amazon River flows about 6,575 kilometers through Peru, Colombia and Brazil and carries by far the largest volume of any river on Earth, draining a rainforest basin long settled by farming and fishing societies before European contact.
facts: The Amazon's length, about 6,575 kilometers, and whether it or the Nile is the world's longest river are disputed depending on which headwater and mouth channels are counted; its average discharge at the delta, about 224,000 cubic meters per second, is unmatched by any other river.

Communities along the river and its floodplains built raised fields, mounds and patches of enriched dark earth from at least the 1st millennium BCE, evidence used to argue for larger and more settled pre-Columbian populations than once assumed.

The Spanish expedition of Francisco de Orellana made the first recorded European descent of the river in 1541 to 1542, reaching its mouth on 24 August 1542; Orellana's account of fighting women warriors is the traditional source of the river's name.

Rubber tapped from Amazonian trees fed a boom from 1879 to 1912 that enriched cities such as Manaus and Iquitos and brought forced labor and violence against Indigenous peoples, with estimates of about 100,000 deaths across the region in that period; the boom collapsed after rubber plantations in Southeast Asia entered the market in 1912.

Deforestation for agriculture, logging and mining has reduced parts of the rainforest, and large dams such as Belo Monte on a major tributary have displaced communities and altered river flow; the extent of long-term ecological damage is debated.
place/amazon-river.context: The Amazon's floodplain was home to Indigenous societies including the Marajoara Culture near its mouth, and the dark-earth soils tied to the Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths event and to societies such as the Casarabe Culture farther upriver. European arrival on the river opened it to the wider Columbian Exchange, and its forests are now central to debates over Modern Climate Change. It sits in the Bronze Age by the date_start used here and the region Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and Earth Systems and Life.
place/amazon-river.observer: The Observer notes that the Amazon's forest was long read by outsiders as nearly empty of large societies, and that raised fields, mounds and dark earth are evidence used to challenge that reading, an example of how a landscape's story-glue can change as new evidence is found. The rubber boom shows an exchange-web reaching into the basin and extracting wealth through sanctioned harm against the people living there, which the Observer records as suffering. The reading would weaken if pre-Columbian populations along the river prove to have been smaller and less settled than the dark-earth evidence suggests.
questions: How large were pre-Columbian populations along the Amazon, and how much of the "pristine forest" idea reflects population loss after 1492 rather than an original absence of large societies?
How much of the river's basin can absorb further deforestation and damming before its water cycle changes significantly?

place/angkor.title: Angkor
place/angkor.summary: Angkor was the capital region of the Khmer Empire in present-day Cambodia, including the temple of Angkor Wat, built in the early 12th century.
facts: Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument in the world by area.
Aerial laser surveys reveal a vast urban area of roughly a thousand square kilometers.
A network of reservoirs (barays) and canals managed water.
It was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992. The traditional date of 1431 for the sack of Angkor by Ayutthaya and its abandonment is now disputed, and Angkor Wat itself was never abandoned.
place/angkor.context: Angkor was the center of the Khmer Empire. See Southeast Asia.
place/angkor.observer: The Observer notes that Angkor was a 'low-density' city, spread over a landscape of water systems and temples, and that it challenges a picture of cities as compact clusters.
questions: What caused the shift of the capital away from Angkor?

place/antarctica.title: Antarctica
place/antarctica.summary: Antarctica is Earth's southernmost continent, with no indigenous population, first sighted by ships in 1820, reached at its geographic pole by Roald Amundsen in 1911, and governed since 1961 under a treaty that reserves it for peaceful, scientific use.
facts: Antarctica covers about 14,200,000 square kilometers under an ice sheet averaging about 1.9 kilometers thick, holding roughly 70 percent of the world's fresh water.

The continent's coast was probably first sighted in 1820 by a Russian expedition under Fabian von Bellingshausen and Mikhail Lazarev, among rival claims from British and American sealers in the same years; the first confirmed landing came in 1895 by a Norwegian party.
Roald Amundsen's Norwegian team reached the geographic South Pole on 14 December 1911, weeks ahead of a British team led by Robert Falcon Scott, whose party died on the return journey.

The Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959 and in force from 1961, bars military activity, mining, and nuclear testing or waste disposal, reserves the continent for peaceful and scientific use, and sets aside territorial claims among its parties.
About 5,000 people work at research stations across Antarctica in the southern summer, falling to about 1,000 in winter.

Warming has been recorded across the continent, with the Antarctic Peninsula's temperature rising by about 3 degrees Celsius since the mid-20th century and the West Antarctic ice sheet losing roughly 100 billion metric tons of ice a year since 2002, contributing to projected sea-level rise.
place/antarctica.context: Antarctic research became a proving ground for international science during the Cold War, alongside the Space Age, and its ice sheet is now a central subject of Modern Climate Change. It sits in the Industrial Age by the date of first sighting and the region Planet-wide, and belongs to the theme threads of Science and Earth Systems and Life.
place/antarctica.observer: The Observer notes that Antarctica is the one large landmass claimed by no kin-lattice of its own, so the claim-lines drawn across it are entirely the product of outside states, and the 1959 treaty is an unusual case of several such states agreeing to set territorial claims aside in favor of shared, peaceful use. The race to the pole in 1911 was a status-signal fought over an empty landscape, and one side's deaths on the return march are recorded here as suffering in the pursuit of that signal. The reading would weaken if the treaty's restraint proves to depend mainly on the continent's low resource value rather than genuine cooperation, a test now approaching as mineral and fishing interest grows.
questions: How long will the Antarctic Treaty's ban on resource extraction hold as demand for minerals and fisheries grows?
How much of the continent's ice loss is now irreversible on a human timescale?

place/arkaim.title: Arkaim
place/arkaim.summary: Arkaim is a fortified Bronze Age settlement of the Sintashta culture in Chelyabinsk Oblast, in the southern Urals of Russia, occupied from about 2000 to 1700 BCE by older reckoning, with a current dating of about 2050 to 1900 BCE.
facts: Archaeologists identified Arkaim in 1987 during surveys ahead of a planned reservoir; the reservoir was cancelled in April 1991 and the site was declared a historical and geographical museum.
Arkaim had a roughly circular plan, on the order of 160 meters across, with concentric walls of earth, timber and clay around houses set in a ring.
Arkaim shows evidence of copper and bronze metalworking, and sites of the same culture in the region are associated with graves holding horses and the earliest known spoke-wheeled chariots.

Arkaim appears to have been abandoned around 1700 BCE, though sources differ on the date; some accounts describe it as burned, and whether by attack, accident or deliberate burning on departure is debated.

Since the 1990s Arkaim has become a tourist and pilgrimage destination and a focus of popular claims that it was an "Aryan" homeland or proto-city, claims that professional archaeologists do not accept as established.
place/arkaim.context: Arkaim is one of the fortified sites of the Sintashta Culture, whose chariot-using elites are often linked, though not conclusively, to early Indo-Iranian speakers discussed under Indo-European Language Spread. It sits in the Bronze Age and the region Central Asian Steppe, and belongs to the theme threads of War and Conflict and Technology.
place/arkaim.observer: The Observer notes that Arkaim, its bronze workshops and the horse-and-chariot graves of its region come from a people with no known mark-code, so everything about them is inferred from soil, metal and bone. The concentric walls are an early durable claim-line on the steppe, and their pairing with elite chariot burials suggests that sanctioned harm was entangled with status-signals. That the site is now used to support identity stories about ancestry shows how a silent place invites story-glue. The reading would weaken if the settlement proves to have been mainly ceremonial or economic rather than defensive.
questions: Was Arkaim mainly a defensive settlement, a ceremonial center or a metalworking town?
Why was Arkaim abandoned around 1700 BCE, and was it burned?

place/athens.title: Athens
place/athens.summary: Athens is a Greek city that, in the 5th century BCE, became the leading city of the Greek world, with an early form of direct democracy and major achievements in philosophy, drama, and art.
facts: Cleisthenes' reforms of about 508 BCE established democratic institutions.
The Parthenon was built between 447 and 432 BCE.
Socrates, Plato, and the tragedians worked in Athens.
Athens lost to Sparta in the Peloponnesian War (431 to 404 BCE).
place/athens.context: Athens was the center of the Ancient Greeks' intellectual world and the base for Aristotle's Lyceum.
place/athens.observer: The Observer notes a small city that produced a disproportionate share of the ideas later taken as foundational. Density of argument seems to matter.
questions: How representative was Athens of Greek city-states?

place/atlantic-ocean.title: Atlantic Ocean
place/atlantic-ocean.summary: The Atlantic Ocean, the second largest of Earth's oceans at about 85 million square kilometers, became from around 1000 CE a corridor for transoceanic voyages that reshaped the connections among Europe, Africa and the Americas.
facts: The Atlantic covers about 85,133,000 square kilometers, has an average depth of about 3,646 meters, and reaches a maximum depth of 8,376 meters in the Puerto Rico Trench.
Norse voyagers were the first people known to have crossed the North Atlantic, reaching Greenland and, around 1000 CE, North America.

Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage opened sustained, repeated crossings between Europe and the Americas, beginning an age of European exploration and colonization that the vault treats through the Columbian Exchange.

From the 16th to the 19th centuries the ocean carried the Atlantic slave trade; estimates for the number of enslaved Africans embarked run to about 12.5 million, of whom roughly 10.7 million are estimated to have survived the crossing.

The first transatlantic telegraph cable operated briefly from August to October 1858 before failing; a successful and lasting cable was laid by the ship Great Eastern in 1866, linking Ireland and Newfoundland by telegraph.
The Atlantic remains central to global shipping and fishing, and its western basin is the source of Atlantic hurricanes that form there in summer and autumn.
place/atlantic-ocean.context: Norse crossings of the Atlantic preceded the far larger movement of people, goods, animals and diseases in the Columbian Exchange, which the ocean also carried the Atlantic Slave Trade across. The 1866 cable was an early feat of the Telegraph and Submarine Cables. It sits in the Medieval Period by its earliest crossing and the region Planet-wide, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and Technology.
place/atlantic-ocean.observer: The Observer notes that the Atlantic went from a barrier crossed rarely and by a few to the busiest exchange-web on the planet within about five centuries, and that the same routes that carried crops, animals and settlers also carried millions of enslaved people, a use of the ocean that the Observer records as sustained, organized harm rather than as a footnote to trade. The 1866 telegraph cable shows the ocean being crossed a third way, by signal rather than by ship, compressing communication from weeks to minutes. The reading would weaken if the Norse voyages prove to have had more lasting exchange with North America than the archaeological record currently shows.
questions: How much contact, if any, did Norse voyagers have with Indigenous peoples of northeastern North America beyond the brief presence recorded at sites like L'Anse aux Meadows?
How did the 1866 telegraph cable change the pace of transatlantic trade and politics in the decades that followed?

place/auschwitz-birkenau.title: Auschwitz-Birkenau
place/auschwitz-birkenau.summary: Auschwitz-Birkenau was a complex of Nazi German concentration and extermination camps near the Polish town of Oświęcim, operated from 1940 to January 1945, where at least 1.1 million people, about 960,000 of them Jews, were murdered.
facts: Auschwitz was established in 1940 near Oświęcim, in Polish territory annexed by Germany, first for Polish political prisoners; the camp at Birkenau (Auschwitz II) was built from 1941 and became a center of mass murder in gas chambers from 1942, and the Monowitz camp (Auschwitz III) supplied forced labor to a chemical works of IG Farben.

About 1.3 million people were deported to Auschwitz and at least 1.1 million of them died; about 960,000 were Jews from across occupied Europe, and other victims included about 74,000 non-Jewish Poles, about 21,000 Roma and Sinti, and about 15,000 Soviet prisoners of war.
Most victims were killed on arrival after selection on the rail platform; others died of forced labor, starvation, disease, shootings and medical experiments.

Prisoners resisted: in October 1944 members of the Sonderkommando revolted and destroyed a crematorium, and escapees, including Witold Pilecki in 1943 and Rudolf Vrba and Alfred Wetzler in 1944, carried reports of the killings to the outside.

As Soviet forces approached in January 1945, the SS forced tens of thousands of prisoners on death marches, and Soviet troops liberated the camp on 27 January 1945, finding about 7,000 prisoners still there.
Auschwitz-Birkenau became a state museum in 1947, and UNESCO inscribed the site in 1979; 27 January is observed as International Holocaust Remembrance Day.
place/auschwitz-birkenau.context: Auschwitz-Birkenau was the largest site of the Holocaust, carried out during World War II. It sits in the Industrial Age and the region Europe, and belongs to the theme threads of War and Conflict and Technology.
place/auschwitz-birkenau.observer: The Observer records Auschwitz-Birkenau as a place where a state murdered more than a million people, most of them Jews, on the basis of an ideology about descent, and records those deaths as suffering and atrocity. The killing was carried out with the methods of administration and industry, rail schedules, selection lists, factories and gas, which shows that tool-lineage and bureaucracy can be turned to sanctioned harm on a very large scale. The preserved site, survivors' testimony and the perpetrators' own records now serve as memory-outsourcing against denial and forgetting, and the resistance of prisoners is part of that record. A historian could challenge the emphasis on administrative method by pointing to the role of ideology and of popular participation, which this account does not explain.
questions: How were the figures for the dead reconstructed, given that the perpetrators destroyed records?
How are survivors' testimony and the physical site being preserved as the last survivors die?

place/ayutthaya.title: Ayutthaya
place/ayutthaya.summary: Ayutthaya is a city on an island at the meeting of three rivers in central Thailand, traditionally founded in 1351, the capital of the Ayutthaya Kingdom until the Burmese army destroyed it in 1767, and a major trading port of Southeast Asia.
facts: Ayutthaya lies on an island at the confluence of the Chao Phraya, Lopburi and Pa Sak rivers, and is traditionally said to have been founded in 1351 (by convention, 4 March 1351) by King U Thong (Ramathibodi I), though the settlement may be older.
In the 1430s Ayutthaya's forces attacked Angkor and installed a short-lived puppet ruler there, though they did not sack the city.

Chinese, Japanese, Persian, Indian and Malay merchants traded at Ayutthaya; the Portuguese, in 1511, were the first Europeans to reach it, the Dutch East India Company opened a trading post in 1608, and King Narai exchanged embassies with the French court in the 1680s.
European visitors in the 17th century described a city of canals, palaces and many temples, and some estimates put its population at several hundred thousand at its height.

A Burmese army besieged Ayutthaya for about 14 months and took it in April 1767, burning much of the city; many thousands of captives were taken to Burma, and much of the kingdom's written record was lost.
Taksin re-established a Siamese state after 1767 and the capital moved to Thonburi and then to Bangkok in 1782.
UNESCO inscribed the Historic City of Ayutthaya in 1991.
place/ayutthaya.context: Ayutthaya was the capital of the Ayutthaya Kingdom, which took over the region of the Khmer Empire and Angkor, and it traded with the Dutch East India Company. It sits in the Medieval Period and the region Southeast Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, War and Conflict and Religion and Belief.
place/ayutthaya.observer: The Observer notes that Ayutthaya was a trading capital built on an island where rivers and canals served as moat, road and marketplace at once, and where merchants of many origins met under one ruler. The destruction of 1767 removed much of the kingdom's own written record, so a large part of what is known about it comes from foreign visitors' accounts, a loss of memory-outsourcing that shapes how the city is understood. The Observer records the taking of captives as suffering as well as loss of skill and labor. The reading would weaken if surviving Thai and Burmese records prove richer than assumed.
questions: How large was Ayutthaya's population at its height?
How much of Ayutthaya's own written record survived 1767, and where is it held?

place/babylon.title: Babylon
place/babylon.summary: Babylon was a city on the Euphrates River in present-day Iraq, first mentioned in the late 3rd millennium BCE, the capital of Hammurabi's kingdom and later of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, and a center of astronomy, law and religion.
facts: Babylon lies near Hillah, about 85 kilometers south of Baghdad, and is first mentioned in a tablet from the late 3rd millennium BCE.
Babylon rose under Hammurabi (reigned about 1792 to 1750 BCE), whose law code was inscribed on a stele found at Susa and now held in the Louvre.
The Hittite king Mursili I sacked Babylon about 1595 BCE, after which the Kassites ruled it for centuries; the Assyrian king Sennacherib destroyed it in 689 BCE, and his son Esarhaddon rebuilt it.
Under Nebuchadnezzar II (reigned 605 to 562 BCE) Babylon had the Ishtar Gate, a large ziggurat called Etemenanki and palaces, and his armies destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BCE.

Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon in 539 BCE; the Cyrus Cylinder, a clay text found there in 1879, presents him as chosen by the god Marduk, and claims that it is a charter of human rights are debated.
Alexander the Great died at Babylon in 323 BCE; the city declined after the Seleucids founded Seleucia on the Tigris.
Babylonian scribes kept the Astronomical Diaries from about 652 to 61 BCE, one of the longest continuous records of celestial observation.
No Babylonian text or archaeological trace has confirmed the Hanging Gardens described by Greek writers; some scholars have proposed that they were at Nineveh.
Military bases of US-led forces at the site in 2003 to 2004 damaged ancient remains, and UNESCO inscribed Babylon in 2019.
place/babylon.context: Babylon's rulers fought the Neo-Assyrian Empire, destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BCE, and lost the city to the Achaemenid Persians and then to Alexander's Conquests. It sits in the Bronze Age and the region Mesopotamia, and belongs to the theme threads of Science, War and Conflict and Religion and Belief.
place/babylon.observer: The Observer notes that Babylon exists in memory in three forms that do not match: the excavated city, the scriptural symbol of exile and pride, and the source of a long astronomical record kept by scribes, an early case of memory-outsourcing in service of pattern-taming. The Hanging Gardens show a story outliving its evidence, since a wonder described by later writers leaves no trace in the city's own records. The reading would weaken if excavation at Babylon or Nineveh finds the gardens.
questions: Where were the Hanging Gardens, if they existed?
How large was Babylon at its height?

place/bagan.title: Bagan
place/bagan.summary: Bagan is an archaeological zone on the Irrawaddy River in central Myanmar, the capital of the Pagan Kingdom from a traditional founding date of 849 CE until the kingdom's collapse in the late 13th century, and the site of thousands of Buddhist monuments.
facts: Bagan lies on the Irrawaddy River in central Myanmar; tradition dates its founding to 849 CE, and it flourished from the 11th to the 13th century.
King Anawrahta (reigned 1044 to 1077) expanded the kingdom and promoted Theravada Buddhism.
More than 10,000 temples, pagodas and monasteries are estimated to have been built on the plain, and about 2,200 survive.

Many monuments were funded by private donors as well as kings, and inscriptions record gifts of land, labor and goods to temples; some historians argue that tax-exempt land grants to religious institutions reduced state revenue, a view that is debated.
Mongol armies defeated Pagan forces at Ngasaunggyan in 1277 and invaded again in 1287, after which the Pagan Kingdom collapsed; Bagan remained a religious center.
Earthquakes have damaged the monuments, including one in 2016 that damaged hundreds of them, and UNESCO inscribed Bagan in 2019.
place/bagan.context: Bagan was the capital of the Pagan Kingdom, which fell after the Mongol Conquests reached Southeast Asia, and it was contemporary with the temple-building of Angkor. It sits in the Medieval Period and the region Southeast Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief, Art and Ritual and War and Conflict.
place/bagan.observer: The Observer notes that Bagan is the result of merit-making at scale: donors turned wealth into religious standing by building temples, and the sheer number of monuments, far beyond what kings alone would need, is a status-signal spread across a whole class of patrons. The proposal that land given to temples weakened the state suggests that a meaning-engine can also drain the institution that supports it, though historians debate the proposal. The reading would weaken if the record shows that temple land was too small a share of the kingdom's land to matter for its revenue.
questions: How much of the Pagan Kingdom's land was held by religious institutions?
How many people lived at Bagan in its 13th-century peak?

place/baghdad.title: Baghdad
place/baghdad.summary: Baghdad is a city on the Tigris River in Iraq, founded in 762 CE by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur as a round capital and, for about five centuries, the seat of the Abbasid caliphs and a leading center of learning.
facts: Baghdad was founded in 762 by the caliph al-Mansur as a round city called Madinat al-Salam ("City of Peace"), near the older Sasanian capital Ctesiphon; no part of the Round City survives above ground.
Baghdad became the center of the Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom, and paper mills were operating there by the 790s.
Population estimates for Baghdad in the 9th and 10th centuries run from several hundred thousand to over a million, which would have made it one of the largest cities in the world.

Baghdad remained the seat of the Abbasid caliphs until 1258, when Mongol forces under Hulagu took the city after a siege and killed the caliph al-Musta'sim; chronicles report figures ranging from 200,000 (Hulagu's own estimate) to as much as 2,000,000 (in Muslim sources), figures modern historians regard as unreliable and likely inflated by later epidemics, though the massacre and destruction were severe.
Baghdad was under Ottoman rule from 1534, with Safavid periods before and after, until British forces captured it in 1917; it became the capital of the Kingdom of Iraq in 1921.
In April 2003, after the US-led invasion, looting of the Iraq National Museum removed about 15,000 objects, some of which have since been recovered.
place/baghdad.context: Baghdad was the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate and the home of the Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom; it was taken in the Mongol Conquests and later ruled by the Ottoman Empire. It sits in the Medieval Period and the region Mesopotamia, and belongs to the theme threads of Science, Trade and Economy and War and Conflict.
place/baghdad.observer: The Observer notes that Baghdad was a planned city that became a knot in an exchange-web: books, translators, paper and scholars from several languages made it a place where Greek, Persian and Indian sources were gathered and rewritten, memory-outsourcing at scale. The Round City itself is now known only from texts, because later buildings covered it, while the losses of 1258 and 2003 show that stored knowledge is exposed to political violence. Historians debate how far the court and how far private patrons drove the translation work, and the reading would weaken if private patronage proves to have been the larger force.
questions: How many people died in the Mongol sack of 1258, and how much of Baghdad's book collection was lost?
How large was Baghdad at its peak?

place/beringia.title: Beringia
place/beringia.summary: Beringia was the land region, including a broad land bridge, that joined northeastern Siberia and Alaska when sea levels were lower during the last ice age, and that later flooded to form the Bering Strait.
facts: Lower sea level during glacial periods exposed the shallow floor of the Bering and Chukchi Seas.
At its widest, the exposed land was more than a thousand kilometers from north to south.
Much of Beringia was cold, dry steppe-tundra that supported mammoths, bison, and horses, and was largely unglaciated.
Genetic evidence suggests ancestors of Native Americans may have been isolated in Beringia for several thousand years before moving south; this is the Beringian standstill hypothesis, still debated.
Rising seas began flooding the land bridge around 11,000 years ago, and it was fully submerged by roughly 10,000 to 9,000 years ago.
place/beringia.context: Beringia is the corridor and refuge at the center of the Peopling of the Americas, and it shaped the movements of animals such as the Woolly Mammoth during the Last Glacial Maximum. Its populations connect to those of Mal'ta and the Ancient North Eurasians. Beringia sits in the Pleistocene Epoch and the region Siberia and the Arctic, and belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life and Kinship and Society.
place/beringia.observer: The Observer notes that a place vanished beneath the sea after serving as a homeland, a highway, and a shelter. What the species calls the origin of the American peoples occurred on ground that no one can now stand on.
questions: How long did populations remain in Beringia, and how did they live?
fact_checks: 2026-09-26: Beringia was an intermittent Pleistocene land connection between northeastern Asia and northwestern North America; the most recent one began to appear about 38,000 years ago and was at its greatest extent about 20,000 years ago, when sea level was lowered by as much as about 120 m, running some 1,600 km north to south; much of it had a dry climate and was not glaciated, with cold-hardy tundra vegetation that let land mammals move into North America [Britannica on Beringia]

place/borobudur.title: Borobudur
place/borobudur.summary: Borobudur is a large Mahayana Buddhist monument in central Java, built around 800 CE under the Sailendra dynasty and often described as the world's largest Buddhist temple.
facts: Construction is dated to roughly the late 8th and early 9th centuries.
The monument has nine stacked platforms and is decorated with 2,672 relief panels and originally 504 Buddha statues.
It was abandoned in the centuries after the shift of power in Java and later covered by vegetation and volcanic ash.
Thomas Stamford Raffles's agent, Hermann Cornelius, cleared the site in 1814.
It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1991 after major restoration.
place/borobudur.context: Borobudur reflects the Buddhist world of Srivijaya and the neighboring Khmer temple-building tradition at Angkor. It represents the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama as a path of ascent. Borobudur sits in the Medieval Period and the region Southeast Asia, and belongs to the theme thread of Religion and Belief and Art and Ritual.
place/borobudur.observer: The Observer notes that a pilgrim walks upward through narrative panels before reaching a summit with no images at all. The architecture is itself an argument about learning: from stories to silence.
questions: Why was the monument abandoned?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Built in the 8th-9th centuries under the Sailendra; 2,672 relief panels and 504 Buddha statues; rediscovered 1814; UNESCO 1991 [World History Encyclopedia on Borobudur]

place/botany-bay.title: Botany Bay
place/botany-bay.summary: Botany Bay is an inlet on the coast of Sydney, Australia, where the Gweagal and Kamaygal peoples lived for thousands of years and where James Cook landed in 1770, though the British colony of 1788 was founded nearby at Port Jackson instead.
facts: Botany Bay lies about 13 kilometers south of central Sydney; the Gweagal lived on its south shore and the Kamaygal on its north, part of a wider set of at least 28 clans in the region, who call the bay Kamay in the Dharawal language, with archaeological evidence of occupation going back some 5,000 years.

James Cook landed at Kurnell on 29 April 1770; he first called the site Stingrays Harbour, then renamed it Botany Bay for the many plants collected there by the naturalists Joseph Banks and Daniel Solander.

Cook's landing party had a brief and wary encounter with local Aboriginal people; when the First Fleet arrived in January 1788, Aboriginal observers were reported as curious but suspicious of the newcomers.

Governor Arthur Phillip found Botany Bay unsuitable for the planned colony because of poor freshwater, shallow anchorage, weak soil and exposed, swampy ground, and on 26 January 1788 he moved the fleet to found the settlement at Sydney Cove on Port Jackson instead.
Sydney Airport now occupies the northwestern shore of the bay, with runways extending into it, and Port Botany is a major container port.
place/botany-bay.context: Botany Bay was long the country of the Aboriginal Australians before Cook's 1770 landing, and the colony that followed at Port Jackson began the First Fleet and the Colonization of Australia. Like Uluru, it is a place where a European-given name sits over a much older Aboriginal name and presence. It sits in the Early Modern Period and the region Oceania, and belongs to the theme threads of War and Conflict and Trade and Economy.
place/botany-bay.observer: The Observer notes that Botany Bay is remembered in outside accounts mainly for a brief 1770 landing and for being passed over in 1788, which risks erasing the much longer claim-line of the Gweagal and Kamaygal who lived there for thousands of years before either visit. The colony's move to Port Jackson was a practical decision about water and anchorage, not a decision about whose country it was, and the disruption that followed for Aboriginal people around Sydney is recorded here as sustained harm, whichever bay the ships used. The reading would weaken if evidence shows more direct conflict at Cook's 1770 landing than the brief, wary encounter usually described.
questions: How did Gweagal and Kamaygal communities understand and respond to Cook's 1770 visit, in their own terms rather than the ship's log?
How did the colony's move to Port Jackson change the impact of British settlement on the peoples of the Botany Bay area compared with what a Botany Bay colony would have done?

place/bukhara.title: Bukhara
place/bukhara.summary: Bukhara is a city in the Zarafshan oasis of Uzbekistan, a Sogdian trading city, capital of the Samanid dynasty, and for more than a thousand years a center of Islamic learning on the Silk Roads.
facts: Bukhara has been settled for a long time; the city celebrated 2,500 years in 1997 on a traditional dating, while archaeological evidence places its walled Sogdian settlement by about the 6th century BCE.
Bukhara was a Sogdian city when Arab armies took it in 709 to 710, and the scholar Muhammad al-Bukhari, compiler of a major collection of hadith, was born there in 810.

Under the Samanid dynasty (819 to 999), Bukhara was a capital of learning and of Persian literature; the physician and philosopher Ibn Sina was born near it in 980, and the Samanid mausoleum was built in the late 9th to 10th century.
The Mongol army under Chinggis Khan took Bukhara in 1220; the city was burned and many of its people were killed or enslaved, though the number is unknown.

The Kalyan Minaret, built in 1127, still stands, and Bukhara was the capital of the Emirate of Bukhara (1785 to 1920), which became a Russian protectorate by 1873 after Russia conquered key Bukharan territories in 1868.
The Red Army took Bukhara in 1920, and the citadel (Ark) was destroyed after four days of fighting.
UNESCO inscribed the Historic Centre of Bukhara in 1993.
place/bukhara.context: Bukhara was a Sogdians city, paired in later history with Samarkand, and it fell to the Mongol Conquests after coming under the world of the Rise of Islam. It sits in Classical Antiquity and the region Central Asian Oases, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, Religion and Belief and Science.
place/bukhara.observer: The Observer notes that Bukhara was taken by a long series of powers, Sogdian, Arab, Samanid, Mongol, Uzbek, Russian and Soviet, yet regained its role as a center of learning after most of them, which suggests that scholars, patrons and trade routes were rebuilt faster than the buildings. Its standing as a place of Islamic scholarship was a story-glue that outlasted each ruler. The reading would weaken if the record shows long gaps in scholarly output after the sack of 1220.
questions: How large was Bukhara before and after the Mongol sack of 1220?
How did scholarship in Bukhara recover after each conquest?

place/cahokia.title: Cahokia
place/cahokia.summary: Cahokia was the largest city of the Mississippian culture, near present-day St. Louis, flourishing from about 1050 to 1350 CE.
facts: At its peak, about 1050 to 1150, it may have held 10,000 to 20,000 people, though some estimates are much higher.
Monks Mound, about 30 meters high, is the largest earthen mound in the Americas.
A circle of posts, known as Woodhenge, likely tracked the sun.
Its population relied on maize agriculture and declined after about 1250, for reasons that are debated. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.
place/cahokia.context: Cahokia is the largest known urban center in pre-Columbian North America north of Mexico. See Domestication of Maize.
place/cahokia.observer: The Observer notes that a city with monumental architecture and no writing left its record in earth. Its size is a reminder that urban life was not limited to the regions usually associated with cities.
questions: Why did Cahokia decline?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Peak population 10,000-20,000 (1050-1150), some estimates higher; Monks Mound about 30 m; UNESCO listing 1982 [UNESCO World Heritage Centre]

place/caral.title: Caral
place/caral.summary: Caral is an ancient city in Peru's Supe Valley, occupied from about 2600 BCE, and one of the oldest known urban centers in the Americas.
facts: Its monumental platform mounds and sunken plazas date to the same era as the Egyptian pyramids.
The society had no pottery and no evidence of large-scale warfare.
Coastal fishing provided anchovies and sardines, and cotton for nets, while inland farming provided crops.
Knotted cords found at the site may be early relatives of the quipu; see Quipu. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009.
place/caral.context: Caral shows The Urban Revolution occurring independently in the Andes, long before the Inca Empire.
place/caral.observer: The Observer notes a city built on a mix of sea and farm foods, with monuments but seemingly little violence. It challenges a picture in which cities depend on grain and conquest.
questions: What held Caral society together without weapons or pottery?

place/carthage.title: Carthage
place/carthage.summary: Carthage was a Phoenician colony on the coast of present-day Tunisia, traditionally founded in 814 BCE, which became a major Mediterranean power until Rome destroyed it in 146 BCE.
facts: It grew into a naval and commercial empire across the western Mediterranean.
Three Punic Wars against Rome were fought between 264 and 146 BCE.
Hannibal crossed the Alps with an army in 218 BCE.
Rome destroyed the city in 146 BCE and later refounded it as a Roman colony. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.
place/carthage.context: Carthage descended from the Phoenicians and lost its long rivalry with the Romans. See Rome.
place/carthage.observer: The Observer notes that most of what is known about Carthage comes from its enemies, since its own records were largely lost. The winners of a war often write the losers' histories.

place/chaco-canyon.title: Chaco Canyon
place/chaco-canyon.summary: Chaco Canyon, in northwestern New Mexico, was the ceremonial and trade center of the Ancestral Puebloan world from about 850 to 1150 CE.
facts: Its 'great houses', such as Pueblo Bonito, had hundreds of rooms.
A network of roads radiated from the canyon.
Buildings and rock carvings align with the sun and moon, such as the 'Sun Dagger' on Fajada Butte.
Chaco is considered sacred by modern Pueblo peoples. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.
place/chaco-canyon.context: Chaco is a major site of the ancient peoples of North America. Its ties to Mesoamerica included traded goods such as macaw feathers and chocolate residues.
place/chaco-canyon.observer: The Observer notes a place built to keep time by the sky. Astronomy and architecture were joined, and the results were legible to those who knew the calendar.
questions: What was the social structure of the Chaco system?

place/chang-an.title: Chang'an
place/chang-an.summary: Chang'an was the capital of the Western Han dynasty from 202 BCE and, in a rebuilt form, of the Sui and Tang dynasties, on the site of present-day Xi'an in Shaanxi, China, until it was dismantled in 904 CE.
facts: Chang'an was founded as the Han capital after 202 BCE, with the Changle Palace completed in 200 BCE; the census of 2 CE recorded about 250,000 residents.
The Sui dynasty built a new planned city, Daxing, southeast of the Han site from 582, and the Tang, from 618, kept its plan and the name Chang'an.

Tang Chang'an was a grid of walled wards, with gates closed at night, enclosing about 78 square kilometers, with a central avenue and two state-supervised markets. Estimates of its population, with suburbs, vary by source, from several hundred thousand up to about one million.

Chang'an received envoys and merchants from Central Asia, Persia, Korea, Japan and Tibet. The monk Xuanzang returned there in 645 with Buddhist texts from India, and the Nestorian Stele, recording a Christian community, was erected there in 781.

Chang'an fell to rebels in 756 during the An Lushan Rebellion and was briefly held by Tibetan forces in 763. In 904 the warlord Zhu Wen forced the court to move to Luoyang and had the city's palaces and houses pulled down.
The plan of Chang'an influenced the layout of the Japanese capitals Nara and Kyoto.
place/chang-an.context: Chang'an was founded just after the fall of the dynasty created by the Unification of China under Qin, and it served as the capital of the Han Dynasty and the Tang Dynasty. It was the eastern end of the routes described in Opening of the Silk Roads, where Sogdians were prominent traders, and its plan was echoed in Nara and Kyoto. Chang'an sits in Classical Antiquity, with its peak in the Medieval Period, in the region East Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, Religion and Belief and Art and Ritual.
place/chang-an.observer: The Observer notes that Tang Chang'an turned social order into geometry: walled wards, gates closed at night, two supervised markets, and one avenue leading to the palace. A plan with claim-lines this exact was later copied at Nara and Kyoto, which suggests that a floor plan can carry story-glue about what a capital should look like. Its end in 904 shows the reverse, that a capital's meaning could be moved by moving the court and taking down the buildings. This reading would weaken if the Japanese copying turns out to have been driven mainly by practical drainage and defense rather than a shared idea of order.
questions: How densely built was Tang Chang'an inside its walls, especially in the southern wards?
How faithfully were the plans of Nara and Kyoto copied from Chang'an, and by what route did the design travel?

place/chauvet-cave.title: Chauvet Cave
place/chauvet-cave.summary: Chauvet Cave in the Ardeche region of southern France contains some of the oldest known figurative paintings, made by early Homo sapiens about 36,000 years ago.
facts: The cave was found in December 1994 by Jean-Marie Chauvet, Eliette Brunel, and Christian Hillaire.
It holds hundreds of paintings and engravings of animals including horses, lions, mammoths, rhinoceroses, and bears.
Radiocarbon dates place the main painted phase at about 37,000 to 33,500 years ago, in the Aurignacian, with a second phase of use about 31,000 to 28,000 years ago.
A rockfall sealed the cave entrance, preserving the art until its discovery.
It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2014; a full-scale replica, the Caverne du Pont d'Arc, opened nearby in 2015.
place/chauvet-cave.context: Chauvet is a benchmark for Emergence of Symbolic Art in Europe, and shows the artistic abilities of early Homo sapiens at a time when the Woolly Mammoth was a common sight on the steppe. Chauvet Cave sits in the Paleolithic and the region Europe, and belongs to the theme thread of Art and Ritual.
place/chauvet-cave.observer: The Observer notes that the earliest painted animals show skilled drawing, not clumsy beginnings, suggesting that a longer tradition lies behind them. Access to the cave is now restricted and a replica is visited instead, a modern echo of the choice to make images rather than only look at the animals.
questions: Were the paintings tied to ritual, storytelling, or something else?

place/chichen-itza.title: Chichen Itza
place/chichen-itza.summary: Chichen Itza is a major Maya-Toltec city on the Yucatan Peninsula that flourished from about 800 to 1100 CE and is known for its stepped pyramid, El Castillo.
facts: It is in the northern Yucatan, where it prospered after many southern lowland cities declined.
El Castillo, the Temple of Kukulcan, has 91 steps on each of its four stairways plus a top platform, totaling 365.
At the spring and autumn equinoxes, sunlight creates a serpent-like shadow on the staircase.
The site has the largest ball court in the Americas, about 166 meters (545 feet) long, and a sacred cenote used for offerings.
It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1988.
place/chichen-itza.context: Chichen Itza thrived as the Classic Maya Collapse reshaped the Maya world, and it is often compared with the later capital Tenochtitlan. Chichen Itza sits in the Medieval Period and the region Mesoamerica, and belongs to the theme thread of Religion and Belief and Art and Ritual.
place/chichen-itza.observer: The Observer notes that the pyramid seems built to put a moving shadow on a staircase at a particular hour, and that visitors gather to watch it today. A structure works as a calendar and a show at once.
questions: How much of the equinox effect was intended?

place/constantinople.title: Constantinople
place/constantinople.summary: Constantinople was founded in 330 CE by Emperor Constantine on the site of Byzantium and served as the capital of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire until the Ottoman conquest in 1453.
facts: The Hagia Sophia was completed in 537 under Emperor Justinian.
The city was sacked by the Fourth Crusade in 1204.
It fell to Mehmed II on 29 May 1453.
It sits on the Bosphorus, between Europe and Asia; it is now Istanbul.
place/constantinople.context: The city outlived the Fall of the Western Roman Empire by almost a thousand years. It later became the capital of the Ottoman Empire.
place/constantinople.observer: The Observer notes that geography kept the city valuable to every ruler. A strait that joins two seas and two continents is a permanent asset.
questions: Was the fall of Constantinople a major turning point or an ending of a long decline?

place/cusco.title: Cusco
place/cusco.summary: Cusco is a city in the Andes of southern Peru, at about 3,400 meters, that Inca tradition says was founded around 1200 CE and that served as the capital of the Inca Empire until the Spanish took it in 1533.
facts: Cusco lies at about 3,400 meters in the Peruvian Andes; Inca tradition credits its founding to Manco Cápac around 1200, but archaeology shows that the Killke culture lived in the region from about 900 to 1200 and that the city grew slowly before Pachacuti.

Under Pachacuti, whose reign is traditionally dated from 1438, and his successors, Cusco was the center of the Inca Empire, with the Coricancha (Temple of the Sun) at its ritual heart and the fortress of Sacsayhuamán above the city.
Spanish accounts, notably Bernabé Cobo's in the 17th century, describe 41 lines called ceques radiating from the Coricancha and linking about 328 shrines (huacas).
Some writers say the city was laid out in the shape of a puma, a claim that remains debated.
Francisco Pizarro's force entered Cusco on 15 November 1533, and Manco Inca besieged the Spanish there for about ten months in 1536 to 1537 without success.

The Spanish built churches and houses on Inca foundations; an earthquake in 1650 destroyed almost all colonial buildings and one in 1950 damaged more than a third of the city's structures, while many Inca walls remained standing.
Túpac Amaru II was executed in Cusco's Plaza de Armas in 1781 during his rebellion against Spanish rule.
UNESCO inscribed Cusco in 1983, and it had 428,450 residents in 2017.
place/cusco.context: Cusco was the capital of the Inca Empire and the seat of Pachacuti, whose reign is linked to the empire's expansion, and it fell in the Spanish Conquest of the Inca Empire. It is the usual gateway to Machu Picchu, and Túpac Amaru II was executed there. Inca administrators kept records on knotted cords, the Quipu. Cusco sits in the Medieval Period and the region Andes, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief, War and Conflict and Art and Ritual.
place/cusco.observer: The Observer notes that Cusco was arranged as a map of belief and rule at once: the ceque lines tied kin groups and shrines to the capital, and the Coricancha placed the ritual center where the emperor's authority sat, a story-glue that could be read by walking the city. Its Inca walls outlasted earthquakes that felled Spanish buildings, and the Spanish built on them, so a later claim-line rests on an earlier one. Much of what is known of the plan comes from Spanish writers with their own aims, since Inca knotted-cord records are only partly understood. The reading would weaken if excavations show the ceque system was less regular than Cobo's account implies.
questions: How regular was the ceque system in practice, and how much of Cobo's account reflects Inca practice rather than Spanish understanding?
How much of Cusco's Inca plan and stonework lies beneath the colonial city?

place/cordoba.title: Córdoba
place/cordoba.summary: Córdoba is a city on the Guadalquivir River in Andalusia, southern Spain, founded by Rome in the 2nd century BCE and best known as the capital of Muslim Iberia and of the Umayyad caliphate of Córdoba (929 to 1031).
facts: Córdoba, Roman Corduba, was founded in the 2nd century BCE (169 or 152 BCE, a contested date), became the colony Colonia Patricia in 46 to 45 BCE and later the capital of the province of Baetica.
Muslim forces took the city in 711 or 712, and in 716 it became the provincial capital of al-Andalus.

Abd al-Rahman I, an Umayyad prince who escaped the dynasty's overthrow by the Abbasids in 750, took power in 756; Abd al-Rahman III declared himself caliph in 929, and the caliphate ended in 1031 when Hisham III was expelled.
The Great Mosque was begun in 785 to 786 and enlarged into the 10th century, and the palace-city of Madinat al-Zahra, begun about 936, was sacked in the civil war of the early 11th century.
Estimates of Córdoba's population around 1000 CE range from about 100,000 to 1,000,000, and medieval accounts credit its libraries with very large collections.

Muslims, Christians and Jews lived in the city under Muslim rule, non-Muslims with a protected but unequal legal status, and historians debate how far the term "convivencia" (coexistence) fits; Ibn Rushd (Averroes) and Moses Maimonides were both born in Córdoba in the 12th century.
Ferdinand III of Castile took the city on 29 June 1236 and the mosque became a cathedral; from 1523 a cathedral nave was built inside it.
UNESCO inscribed the Mosque-Cathedral in 1984 and extended the listing to the whole historic center in 1994.
place/cordoba.context: Córdoba was a provincial capital of the Romans before it became the seat of the Umayyad Caliphate's Iberian branch in Al-Andalus, a state that claimed the caliphate in rivalry with the Abbasid Caliphate. Its conquest belongs to the Rise of Islam. Córdoba sits in Classical Antiquity by its earliest founding, with its peak in the Medieval Period, in the region Mediterranean Basin, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief, Art and Ritual and Science.
place/cordoba.observer: The Observer notes that the Great Mosque of Córdoba carries several claim-lines in one structure: a Muslim ruler's place of worship enlarged over two centuries, then a cathedral with a nave set inside it, so the building itself records who held the city in each period. A court that gathered scholars, books and craftsmen while claiming the caliphate was making a status-signal aimed at rival caliphs; because the figures for the city's size and libraries are uncertain, the reading rests on the building more than on numbers. The reading would weaken if the court's patronage proves to have been driven mainly by internal politics.
questions: How large was Córdoba in the 10th century, given estimates that differ by a factor of ten?
How did Muslims, Christians and Jews live alongside one another in practice, and how did that change?

place/doggerland.title: Doggerland
place/doggerland.summary: Doggerland was a lowland region of hunter-gatherers that connected Britain to continental Europe and lay where the North Sea is today until it was gradually flooded by rising seas.
facts: After the last ice age, sea level rose as ice sheets melted, and the land now under the southern North Sea was progressively submerged.

It was largely underwater by around 6000 BCE, though a 2020 study argues that remnant islands survived for centuries after the tsunami and that the last land was submerged about a thousand years later.
The Storegga Slide, a huge submarine landslide off Norway, produced a tsunami around 6200 BCE that struck the coasts of the region.
Fishing vessels have dredged up animal bones and worked bone points from the seabed, and surveys have mapped submerged river valleys.
Its inhabitants were Mesolithic hunter-gatherers.
place/doggerland.context: Doggerland is a European counterpart to Beringia, a lost landscape drowned by post-glacial sea-level rise, and it followed the Last Glacial Maximum and the Younger Dryas. Doggerland sits in the Neolithic and the region Europe, and belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
place/doggerland.observer: The Observer notes that a landscape once lived on by humans now lies under fishing grounds and wind farms, its record kept only as tools brought up in nets. The land bridge between Britain and Europe is a reminder that coastlines are provisional.
questions: How large was the population, and how did it respond to rising water?

place/elmina-castle.title: Elmina Castle
place/elmina-castle.summary: Elmina Castle is a fortress on the coast of Ghana built by the Portuguese in 1482 as São Jorge da Mina, the first European fort on the Gulf of Guinea, and later a holding place for people sold into the Atlantic slave trade.
facts: Elmina Castle stands at the town of Elmina in Ghana's Central Region; the Portuguese built it in 1482 by agreement with local rulers, to trade for gold, and named it São Jorge da Mina ("Saint George of the Mine").
In the 16th century the Portuguese also brought enslaved people to Elmina from elsewhere on the African coast and exchanged them for gold with African traders.

The Dutch captured Elmina in 1637, and Portugal ceded its claims in 1642; under Dutch rule the castle became a base of the Dutch West India Company, whose trade came to include large-scale export of enslaved people to the Americas.
Enslaved people were held in dungeons in the castle before being shipped across the Atlantic; the total number who passed through Elmina is unknown.
Britain took over the Dutch Gold Coast possessions in 1872, and Ghana became independent in 1957.
UNESCO inscribed the Forts and Castles of Ghana, including Elmina, in 1979.
Elmina Castle is now a museum and memorial, and Ghana's "Year of Return" in 2019 drew large numbers of visitors from the African diaspora.
place/elmina-castle.context: Elmina Castle was a node of the Atlantic Slave Trade, which ended in its legal form with the Abolition of Slavery, and Ghana's independence in 1957 belongs to the wider story of Decolonization. It sits in the Early Modern Period and the region Sub-Saharan Africa, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and War and Conflict.
place/elmina-castle.observer: The Observer notes that Elmina began as a fortified place for trading gold and became a holding place for people sold as commodities, so one set of walls served two exchange-webs in sequence. The Observer records the suffering of those held in its dungeons and shipped across the Atlantic, and notes that the site now works as a memorial where descendants come to mark losses for which few individual records survive, a grief-rite built around a building. The reading would weaken if better records show that most enslaved people shipped from the Gold Coast passed through other forts and not through Elmina.
questions: How many people passed through Elmina Castle on their way to the Americas?
How did the local town of Elmina take part in the trade and change because of it?

place/forbidden-city.title: Forbidden City
place/forbidden-city.summary: The Forbidden City is the former imperial palace complex at the center of Beijing, China, built from 1406 to 1420 for the Ming dynasty and used as the residence and ceremonial center of Ming and Qing emperors until 1924.
facts: The Forbidden City was built under the Yongle Emperor from 1406 to 1420, as part of his move of the Ming capital from Nanjing to Beijing.
Twenty-four emperors, 14 Ming and 10 Qing, lived and ruled there.
The Forbidden City covers about 72 hectares, is surrounded by walls about 8 meters high and a moat, and has roughly 980 surviving buildings arranged along a north-south axis.
Commoners were barred from entering, and yellow glazed roof tiles were reserved for imperial use.
Puyi, the last Qing emperor, abdicated in 1912 after the Xinhai Revolution but was allowed to remain in the Inner Court until 1924, when he was expelled; the Palace Museum opened in 1925.

Part of the palace collection was moved south from 1933 to escape Japanese advances, and some of it was taken to Taiwan in 1948 and 1949, where it forms the core of the National Palace Museum in Taipei.
UNESCO inscribed the imperial palaces of Beijing in 1987.
place/forbidden-city.context: The Forbidden City was the palace of the Ming Dynasty and the Qing Dynasty, and the imperial system it housed ended with the Xinhai Revolution. It sits in the Medieval Period and the region East Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Art and Ritual, Religion and Belief and Kinship and Society.
place/forbidden-city.observer: The Observer notes that the Forbidden City is rank made into architecture: nested walls and courtyards on one axis, restricted gates and reserved roof colors, so that a visitor's position in the plan matched their position in the court. Its story-glue was the idea of the emperor as the link between heaven and earth at the center of the world, which the layout was built to state. The same walls now admit visitors by ticket in the millions, so the site's function has shifted from limiting access to displaying a dynastic past as national heritage. A historian could weaken this reading by showing that the layout followed earlier palace conventions and practical needs more than a deliberate message.
questions: How much of the standing Forbidden City dates from the original Ming construction, given repeated fires and rebuilding?
How did the ceremonial use of the palace change between the Ming and the Qing?

place/ganges-river.title: Ganges River
place/ganges-river.summary: The Ganges River (Ganga) is a river of northern India and Bangladesh about 2,525 kilometers long, flowing from the Himalaya to the Bay of Bengal, whose plain has supported some of South Asia's densest populations and which is sacred in Hinduism.
facts: The Ganges rises at the Gangotri glacier in the Himalaya and crosses the northern Indian plain to the Bay of Bengal, where together with the Brahmaputra and Meghna it forms the world's largest delta; its basin supports several hundred million people.
Farming communities occupied the middle Ganges plain from at least the 2nd millennium BCE, and the river became the axis of the later Vedic states and of 1st-millennium BCE kingdoms such as Magadha.

In Hinduism the river is worshiped as the goddess Ganga; ashes of the dead are immersed in it, pilgrims bathe at sites such as Varanasi, and the Kumbh Mela at Prayagraj, where the Ganges meets the Yamuna, draws tens of millions of people.
Sewage and industrial waste pollute long stretches of the river; India launched the Ganga Action Plan in 1985 and the Namami Gange program in 2014, and water quality remains poor in many stretches.
The Farakka Barrage, completed in 1975, diverts water and has been a source of dispute between India and Bangladesh, and a treaty of 1996 governs the sharing of the river's dry-season flow.
In 2017 a High Court in Uttarakhand declared the Ganges and Yamuna to be legal persons, and the Supreme Court of India stayed the ruling.
place/ganges-river.context: The Ganges River was the setting of the Vedic Period as it moved east and of later states such as the Maurya Empire; Varanasi is its most important sacred city. It sits in the Bronze Age (its early farming communities) and the region South Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life, Religion and Belief and Trade and Economy.
place/ganges-river.observer: The Observer notes that the Ganges is treated both as a resource and as a person, and that the two views collide in its condition: a river that is worshiped is also a sewer for millions, which suggests that reverence and upkeep are separate things. A river that crosses a national border shows that religious and hydrological geography does not follow state claim-lines, as the Farakka dispute shows. The reading would weaken if measurements show that ritual practice contributes little to the river's pollution compared with sewage and industry.
questions: How much do religious practices contribute to the pollution of the Ganges compared with sewage and industry?
How will the river's flow change as Himalayan glaciers shrink?

place/giza-necropolis.title: Giza Necropolis
place/giza-necropolis.summary: The Giza Necropolis, near Cairo, holds three large pyramids built for the pharaohs Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure in the 26th century BCE, along with the Great Sphinx.
facts: The Great Pyramid of Khufu was originally about 146.6 meters high.
It was the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years.
Workers were organized labor teams and were fed and housed by the state.
It is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still largely standing.
place/giza-necropolis.context: The complex reflects the power of the Ancient Egyptians state that arose from Unification of Egypt.
place/giza-necropolis.observer: The Observer notes the scale of investment in a tomb: a state that could mobilize thousands for a decade of work on a single ritual object.
questions: How were the stones raised and placed?

place/goree-island.title: Gorée Island
place/goree-island.summary: Gorée Island is a small island off Dakar, Senegal, held in turn by the Portuguese, Dutch, British and French from the 15th century, and a symbol of the Atlantic slave trade, though historians debate how many enslaved people left from it.
facts: Gorée Island lies about 2 kilometers off Dakar; the Portuguese landed in 1444, the Dutch held the island by 1628 (exactly when and how they replaced the Portuguese is unknown, since the early Dutch West India Company archive was largely lost), and the French captured it from the Dutch in 1677, after which control passed between Britain and France several times over the following century.

Gorée was a trading post for goods such as gum and hides and for enslaved people; a community of Afro-European merchant women, called signares, ran trade and property on the island, and some owned enslaved people.
The House of Slaves, built by Nicolas Pépin at a date given variously as about 1776 or 1780 to 1784, and having a doorway to the sea called the "Door of No Return", is a pilgrimage site for visitors.

Many historians argue that Gorée was a modest embarkation point compared with larger ports on the Atlantic coast and that the House of Slaves did not hold the numbers often claimed, while others stress its symbolic importance; the debate is unresolved.
African merchants and rulers took part in the trade alongside European ones.
Visitors to Gorée have reportedly included Nelson Mandela and Pope John Paul II, and, most firmly documented, US President Barack Obama in 2013.
UNESCO inscribed the Island of Gorée in 1978.
place/goree-island.context: Gorée Island was a small port within the Atlantic Slave Trade, which ended in its legal form with the Abolition of Slavery. It sits in the Medieval Period (its first European contact) and the region Sub-Saharan Africa, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, Kinship and Society and War and Conflict.
place/goree-island.observer: The Observer notes that Gorée is a case where a place's symbolic weight and its documented role differ: as a memorial it commemorates the whole of the Atlantic slave trade, while the records suggest that a smaller share of captives left from it than from larger ports. Both can be held at once, since a memorial's function as a grief-rite does not depend on the count, and the Observer records the suffering of the enslaved without ranking sites by numbers. The signares show a kin-lattice and property system in which African women held power within the trade, a reminder that the trade was embedded in local societies. The reading would weaken if new archival counts show that Gorée handled a much larger share of the trade than the current estimates suggest.
questions: How many enslaved people left from Gorée, and in what years?
How should memorial sites present both their documented role and their symbolic one?

place/great-wall-of-china.title: Great Wall of China
place/great-wall-of-china.summary: The Great Wall of China is a series of walls, ditches, towers and forts built across northern China by successive states and dynasties from about the 7th century BCE to the 17th century CE, mainly to control movement between farming societies and the steppe.
facts: The Great Wall began as separate walls built by Warring States kingdoms such as Qi, Yan, Zhao and Qin from about the 7th century BCE (the dating of the earliest walls is uncertain); after unifying China in 221 BCE, Qin Shi Huang linked and extended walls in the north.
The Han dynasty extended walls and signal towers far to the northwest along the Gansu corridor, to protect the routes westward and to counter the Xiongnu.
The best-known standing sections, in brick and stone, date to the Ming dynasty (1368 to 1644), and building intensified after Mongol forces captured the Ming emperor Zhengtong at Tumu in 1449.
A Chinese government survey published in 2012 reported about 21,000 kilometers of walls, trenches and natural barriers built across all dynasties, of which about 8,850 kilometers are Ming.
Soldiers, conscripted laborers and convicts built the wall; how many died is unknown, and the large figures in later stories are not documented.
UNESCO inscribed the Great Wall in 1987. The claim that it is visible to the naked eye from the Moon is false.
place/great-wall-of-china.context: The Great Wall of China links the Unification of China under Qin, the Han Dynasty, the Xiongnu and the Ming Dynasty, and it protected routes used in Opening of the Silk Roads. It sits in the Iron Age (its earliest walls), in the region East Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of War and Conflict, Technology and Trade and Economy.
place/great-wall-of-china.observer: The Observer notes that the Great Wall of China is a claim-line built at very large scale, yet it worked less as a sealed barrier than as a filter, with towers, garrisons and gates that let a state watch and tax movement between two ways of living. The image of one unbroken wall is partly a later story-glue, and some historians argue it grew mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries as a national symbol. Specialists could weaken this reading by showing that the wall's military effect was larger than a filtering account allows.
questions: How much did the walls change frontier outcomes compared with diplomacy and regulated trade?
How many people worked on and died building each major section of the Great Wall?

place/great-zimbabwe.title: Great Zimbabwe
place/great-zimbabwe.summary: Great Zimbabwe was a large stone-walled capital city in southeastern Africa, occupied from about the 11th to 15th century CE, ancestral to the Shona-speaking peoples.
facts: Its Great Enclosure has dry-stone walls up to about 11 meters high.
Older estimates gave 10,000 to 20,000 people; more recent modeling suggests the population did not exceed about 10,000.
It traded gold and ivory with the Swahili coast and beyond.
The modern country Zimbabwe is named after it.
place/great-zimbabwe.context: The city is part of the history of the Bantu Expansion and of Indian Ocean trade linked to Sub-Saharan Africa.
place/great-zimbabwe.observer: The Observer notes that colonial-era writers sometimes denied its African origin, a mistake corrected by archaeology. A monument's meaning can be distorted by those who describe it.
questions: What was the political structure of the city?

place/gobekli-tepe.title: Göbekli Tepe
place/gobekli-tepe.summary: Göbekli Tepe is a Pre-Pottery Neolithic site in southeastern Turkey with large carved T-shaped stone pillars, dating to about 9500 to 8000 BCE.
facts: Pillars stand up to about 5.5 meters tall and are carved with animals.
It was built by people who were, at the time, foragers or early farmers.
Excavations led by Klaus Schmidt began in 1995.
It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2018.
place/gobekli-tepe.context: Göbekli Tepe raises questions about the order of events in The Agricultural Revolution. Compare Çatalhöyük.
place/gobekli-tepe.observer: The Observer notes that monumental construction may have preceded farming, so the labor of building shared sacred places may have helped bring people together.
questions: Was Göbekli Tepe a temple, a gathering place, or something else?

place/harappa.title: Harappa
place/harappa.summary: Harappa is an archaeological site in Punjab, Pakistan, on a dry bed of the Ravi River, occupied from about 3300 BCE and a major city of the Indus Valley Civilization until its urban phase declined after about 1900 BCE.
facts: Harappa was occupied from about 3300 BCE, and its urban "Mature Harappan" phase ran from about 2600 to 1900 BCE, with population estimates ranging from as many as 23,500 in site-specific studies to a wider 30,000 to 60,000 suggested for the largest Indus cities generally.
Harappa had planned streets, brick drains and standardized weights, and its bricks followed a common size ratio used at other Indus sites.

Harappa's seals, carved with animals and signs in a script that has not been deciphered, are found in many Indus cities, and Indus objects such as seals and carnelian beads have been found in Mesopotamian cities.
Daya Ram Sahni began excavations at Harappa in 1921, after British engineers had taken bricks from the site in the 1850s for railway ballast.
The city's urban phase declined after about 1900 BCE, and occupation continued at a smaller scale; proposed causes include changes in monsoon rainfall and river courses, and the causes are debated.
place/harappa.context: Harappa gave its name to the Indus Valley Civilization, whose other great city was Mohenjo-daro, and its planned streets belong to the story of The Urban Revolution. It sits in the Bronze Age and the region South Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, Technology and Language and Writing.
place/harappa.observer: The Observer notes that Harappa left thousands of inscribed seals that cannot yet be read, so its people's own account of themselves is missing, and what is known of its order comes from bricks, weights and drains that suggest a shared administrative logic. The lack of obvious palaces or royal tombs has led some scholars to propose that its rule differed from that of contemporary Mesopotamia and Egypt, though the proposal is debated. The reading would weaken if the script is deciphered and shows a more conventional royal order.
questions: What do the signs on the Harappan seals say?
Why did the urban phase of Harappa decline after about 1900 BCE?

place/hattusa.title: Hattusa
place/hattusa.summary: Hattusa was the capital of the Hittite Empire, at Boğazkale in central Turkey, made the royal seat in about 1650 BCE and abandoned around 1200 BCE, and it preserved an archive of about 30,000 clay tablets.
facts: Hattusa lies at Boğazkale in Çorum Province, Turkey; a Hattian settlement existed there earlier, and King Hattusili I made it the Hittite capital in about 1650 BCE.
Hattusa was ringed by walls with monumental gates, including the Lion Gate and the Sphinx Gate, and had a Great Temple and a nearby rock sanctuary at Yazılıkaya.
The capital moved briefly to Tarhuntassa under Muwatalli II and returned to Hattusa under Mursili III.

Excavators, beginning with Hugo Winckler in 1906, found about 30,000 clay tablets in the royal archives, written in Hittite, Akkadian, Luwian, Hurrian and other languages and holding treaties, rituals and letters, including a version of the treaty with Egypt made after the Battle of Kadesh.
Bedřich Hrozný identified Hittite as an Indo-European language in 1915.
Hattusa was abandoned around 1200 BCE, during the Bronze Age Collapse; its central buildings burned, though whether the city was abandoned before or after the fire is debated.
UNESCO inscribed Hattusha in 1986.
place/hattusa.context: Hattusa was the capital of the Hittites, whose army fought at the Battle of Kadesh and whose empire ended in the Bronze Age Collapse. The Hittite language recorded in its archive is central to the study of the Indo-European Language Spread. Hattusa sits in the Bronze Age and the region Levant and Anatolia, and belongs to the theme threads of War and Conflict, Language and Writing and Religion and Belief.
place/hattusa.observer: The Observer notes that Hattusa is a case of memory-outsourcing at imperial scale: a state kept its treaties, rituals and letters on clay in several languages, and the archive survived in part because fire hardens clay, so the destruction of the city helped preserve its records. Treaties written in the diplomatic language of the day, Akkadian, show rulers of rival powers binding one another with story-glue in the form of oaths sworn before gods. The archive records what the palace chose to keep, and the reading would weaken if the tablets prove to reflect chance survival more than the state's actual priorities.
questions: Why was Hattusa abandoned, and was it burned before or after it was left?
How large was the population of Hattusa at its peak?
