place/havana.title: Havana
place/havana.summary: Havana is the capital of Cuba, on the island's northwest coast, established on its present harbor site in 1519 and long the assembly point for Spanish treasure fleets crossing the Atlantic.
facts: Havana was founded as San Cristóbal de la Habana; the settlement moved twice and was established on its present harbor site in 1519.

From the 1560s Spanish fleets carrying silver from Mexico and Peru assembled at Havana for the crossing to Spain, and the city was fortified with La Real Fuerza (built 1558 to 1577) and El Morro (built 1589 to 1630).
Britain captured Havana after a siege in 1762 during the Seven Years' War and returned it to Spain in 1763 in exchange for Florida; Spain then built the La Cabaña fortress.

Sugar and coffee plantations, worked by enslaved people, expanded Cuba's economy from the late 18th century; hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans arrived in Cuba, many through Havana, and slavery there was abolished in 1886.
The US battleship Maine exploded in Havana harbor on 15 February 1898, killing about 260 crew, an event that helped lead to the Spanish-American War.
Since 1959 Havana has been the capital of a socialist state, and the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 placed Cuba at the center of the Cold War.
UNESCO inscribed Old Havana and its fortifications in 1982.
place/havana.context: Havana was a key port for the silver flow from Potosi and the mainland, for the Sugar Plantation Complex and for the Atlantic Slave Trade, and it changed hands during the Seven Years' War. It was a focal point of the Cold War. Havana sits in the Early Modern Period and the region Caribbean and Atlantic World, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and War and Conflict.
place/havana.observer: The Observer notes that Havana grew because a state needed a fixed place to gather and guard a moving stream of wealth: silver had to be assembled somewhere before the crossing, and fortifications followed the cargo. Its later wealth from sugar rested on enslaved labor, which the Observer records as suffering and not only as an economic input. The waterfront was claimed in turn by the leading naval power of each era, and a historian could challenge this by showing that local Creole elites and enslaved people shaped the city as much as outside powers did.
questions: How many enslaved Africans passed through Havana, and how did their labor shape the city?
How did the treasure-fleet system change the size and character of the city?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Diego Velazquez first founded Havana in 1514 on the opposite coast, about 69 km south of its current location, and the town that became Havana originated beside Puerto de Carenas in 1519 [Wikipedia on Havana]

2026-09-27: A British fleet arrived off Havana on 6 June 1762, and the treaty of 1763 ceded Spanish Florida to Britain in exchange for the return of Havana to Spain, after which the Fortress of San Carlos de la Cabana was begun [Wikipedia on Havana]

2026-09-27: The organised system of Spanish convoys dates from 1564, with fleets rendezvousing at Havana before returning together to Spain carrying silver from Mexico and Peru [Wikipedia on Spanish treasure fleet]

2026-09-27: An explosion on the USS Maine in Havana harbor on 15 February 1898 killed 268 sailors and contributed to the outbreak of the Spanish-American War in April, though the cause remains debated [Wikipedia on USS Maine (ACR-1)]

place/hegra.title: Hegra
place/hegra.summary: Hegra, also called Mada'in Salih, is an archaeological site in the AlUla region of northwestern Saudi Arabia, the second major city of the Nabataean kingdom after Petra, known for 111 monumental rock-cut tombs.
facts: Hegra lies north of the AlUla oasis on a caravan route between southern Arabia and the Mediterranean, and was part of the Nabataean kingdom from about the 1st century BCE.
UNESCO records 111 monumental tombs cut into sandstone outcrops, 94 of them with decorated facades, along with dozens of wells; it inscribed Hegra in 2008, the first UNESCO site in Saudi Arabia.
Many tombs bear Nabataean inscriptions naming the owner and family, forbidding sale or reuse, and threatening penalties or curses; dated inscriptions fall mostly in the 1st century CE.
After Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106 CE, Hegra became part of the province of Arabia, and Roman inscriptions record a military presence there in the 2nd century.
Islamic tradition associates the site with the people of Thamud mentioned in the Quran, and travelers traditionally avoided it.
The Ottoman Hejaz Railway built a station at Mada'in Salih in 1907 to 1908.
place/hegra.context: Hegra was a city of the Nabataeans alongside Petra, on the routes of the Incense Trade, and was absorbed by the Romans. It sits in Classical Antiquity and the region Arabian Peninsula, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and Art and Ritual.
place/hegra.observer: The Observer notes that at Hegra a claim-line is engraved beside the grave: tomb inscriptions record who may be buried, who may not sell, and what penalty follows, so that property law reached past death in stone. A trading people put its most durable writing into grief-rites and inheritance, while most of its everyday commercial records have not survived. The reading rests on the surviving inscriptions being representative of Nabataean practice, which is uncertain because they come from a few unusually well-preserved sites.
questions: How did Hegra's population and economy compare with those of Petra?
How were the tomb inscriptions enforced in practice?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Extensive settlement of Hegra took place in the 1st century CE under the Nabataean king Aretas IV (9 BC to 40 AD), who made it the kingdom's second capital, and it is described as the kingdom's southernmost and second-largest city after Petra [Wikipedia on Hegra]
2026-09-27: UNESCO proclaimed the site a World Heritage Site in 2008, making it Saudi Arabia's first [Wikipedia on Hegra]

2026-09-27: Tomb inscriptions functioned as legal documents recording ownership, burial rights, prohibitions, and dates based on the reigns of Nabataean kings [Wikipedia on Hegra]

2026-09-27: Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106 CE under Trajan and Hegra became part of the province of Arabia, with Legio III Cyrenaica attested there, a Roman inscription of 175 to 177 CE, and the army gone by the late 2nd or early 3rd century [Wikipedia on Hegra]

place/hiroshima.title: Hiroshima
place/hiroshima.summary: Hiroshima is a city on the delta of the Ōta River in western Honshu, Japan, founded as a castle town in 1589 and, on 6 August 1945, the first city struck by a nuclear weapon.
facts: Hiroshima was founded as a castle town in 1589 by the daimyo Mōri Terumoto and grew into a military and port center; its population before the bombing was about 350,000.
At 8:15 a.m. on 6 August 1945 the US B-29 Enola Gay dropped a uranium bomb, "Little Boy", which exploded about 600 meters above the city.

About 70,000 to 80,000 people are estimated to have been killed immediately, and total deaths by the end of 1945 are estimated at 90,000 to 166,000, from burns, injuries and radiation. The dead included civilians, soldiers, Korean forced laborers and a small number of Allied prisoners of war.

Survivors, called hibakusha, faced radiation illness, increased cancer risks and discrimination; the Atomic Bomb Casualty Commission began long-term studies of them in 1947, continued by the Radiation Effects Research Foundation.
A second atomic bomb was dropped on Nagasaki on 9 August, and Japan announced its surrender on 15 August 1945; whether the bombings were necessary to end the war remains debated among historians.
The ruined Genbaku Dome was preserved as a memorial within the Peace Memorial Park, and UNESCO inscribed it in 1996.
place/hiroshima.context: Hiroshima was the target of the first nuclear attack of World War II and gave its name to the beginning of the Nuclear Age. The city of Kyoto had been on the list of possible targets and was removed from it. Hiroshima sits in the Early Modern Period and the region East Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of War and Conflict and Science.
place/hiroshima.observer: The Observer notes that Hiroshima marks the first use of a nuclear weapon against a city, in a single morning, and records the deaths as suffering that continued for decades among survivors. The city has since turned its ruined center into a memorial, keeping the shell of one building standing and collecting survivors' testimony, a grief-rite and an act of memory-outsourcing meant to reach people who were not there. Historians disagree about whether the bombing was necessary to end the war, and this reading takes no side in that dispute. It would weaken if the memorial's message proves to matter less to visitors than to the city that built it.
questions: How many people died in Hiroshima by the end of 1945, and how many later of radiation-related causes?
How has the memory of the bombing been taught and contested in Japan and elsewhere?

2026-09-27: At 8:15 a.m. on 6 August 1945 the American B-29 Enola Gay dropped the enriched-uranium gun-type bomb Little Boy on Hiroshima, which detonated at an altitude of approximately 600 meters (1,900 feet). [Wikipedia on Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki]

2026-09-27: The Hiroshima bombing directly killed at least 70,000 people, and deaths there over the following two to four months are estimated at 90,000 to 166,000, including about 10,000 soldiers and 12 Allied prisoners of war, with some 90 percent of the dead civilians (the Hiroshima article gives a lower total of 90,000 to 140,000). [Wikipedia on Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki; Wikipedia on Hiroshima]

2026-09-27: The A-Bomb Dome, part of the Hiroshima Peace Memorial, has been a World Heritage Site since 1996. [Wikipedia on Hiroshima]

place/hispaniola.title: Hispaniola
place/hispaniola.summary: Hispaniola is the second-largest island of the Caribbean, in the Greater Antilles, divided between Haiti in the west and the Dominican Republic in the east, and the site of the first lasting European settlement in the Americas.
facts: Hispaniola covers about 76,000 square kilometers; its features include Pico Duarte, reported at about 3,101 meters, the highest peak in the Caribbean, and Lake Enriquillo, a saline lake whose depth below sea level is not firmly established by the sources consulted.

The earliest evidence of human presence on Hispaniola is dated by many archaeologists to about 4000 BCE, though estimates vary; by 1492 the island was home to Taíno societies organized into several chiefdoms, and Spanish chroniclers report the names Ayiti, Quisqueya and Bohío for it.
Columbus reached Hispaniola in December 1492, and the Spanish founded La Navidad (destroyed in 1493), La Isabela (1493) and Santo Domingo (1498).
The Taíno population of Hispaniola declined sharply after 1492 under forced labor, violence and disease.
In 1697 Spain ceded the western third of Hispaniola to France, which developed the sugar and slave colony of Saint-Domingue; the Haitian Revolution (1791 to 1804) ended slavery and French rule there.
The Dominican Republic became independent in 1844, after Haitian rule over the whole island from 1822.
place/hispaniola.context: Hispaniola links the Taino, the Columbian Exchange, the city of Santo Domingo, the Sugar Plantation Complex and the Haitian Revolution. It sits in the Neolithic (its earliest human presence) and the region Caribbean and Atlantic World, and belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life, Trade and Economy and War and Conflict.
place/hispaniola.observer: The Observer notes that one island now holds two states, two languages and two colonial histories because a treaty between distant European powers drew a claim-line through it in 1697, with no reference to anything on the island. Hispaniola compresses the Atlantic system into one place, with an indigenous society, a first European base, a plantation colony built on enslaved labor and a successful revolution of enslaved people that founded a state, all within about three centuries. The pattern is not unique, since other Caribbean islands show parts of it, and a specialist could weaken the reading by showing that Hispaniola was more exceptional or more ordinary than it suggests.
questions: When did people first reach Hispaniola, and from where?
How large was the Taíno population of the island in 1492?

place/isfahan.title: Isfahan
place/isfahan.summary: Isfahan is a city on the Zayande River in central Iran, a Seljuk capital from 1051 and the capital of the Safavid Empire from 1598, when Shah Abbas I rebuilt its center around the great square Naqsh-e Jahan.
facts: Isfahan stands on the Zayande River on the Iranian Plateau and was settled long before Islam; it became a Seljuk capital in 1051, and its Friday Mosque reflects more than a thousand years of mosque architecture (UNESCO inscribed it in 2012).
After a revolt in 1387, Timur's forces killed a large part of Isfahan's population; chroniclers give figures of tens of thousands.
Shah Abbas I moved the Safavid capital from Qazvin to Isfahan in 1598 and built the Naqsh-e Jahan (Imam) Square, the Shah and Sheikh Lotfollah mosques, the Ali Qapu palace and covered markets.
Estimates by 17th-century European visitors put Isfahan's population at several hundred thousand, and a Persian saying called the city "half the world".

In 1604 to 1605 Shah Abbas forcibly moved many Armenians from Julfa on the Aras River into Safavid territory, and many died on the way; the survivors founded New Julfa, an Armenian quarter of Isfahan, in about 1606.
Afghan forces under Mahmud Hotak besieged Isfahan in 1722, and the resulting famine killed many tens of thousands of its inhabitants; the fall of the city was a decisive blow to Safavid rule.
Isfahan ceased to be the capital in the 18th century, and UNESCO inscribed Meidan Emam, Esfahan in 1979.
place/isfahan.context: Isfahan was the capital of the Safavid Empire, a rival of the Ottoman Empire, and it had earlier suffered the massacre ordered by Timur, founder of the Timurid Empire. It sits in the Medieval Period and the region Iranian Plateau, and belongs to the theme threads of Art and Ritual, Religion and Belief and Trade and Economy.
place/isfahan.observer: The Observer notes that Isfahan under Shah Abbas is a capital designed as a display: a square where a palace, a royal mosque and a merchants' bazaar face one another, placing the ruler's authority, the religious establishment and commerce in one visible arrangement, a status-signal in urban form. The same ruler's forced movement of the Armenians, which the Observer records as suffering, produced a prosperous merchant community that traded silk across Eurasia, an exchange-web outcome of coercion. The reading would weaken if the wealth of New Julfa proves to have come mainly from trading networks that existed before Safavid patronage.
questions: How large was Isfahan's population at its peak?
How many Armenians died during the deportation from Julfa?

place/issyk-kul.title: Issyk-Kul
place/issyk-kul.summary: Issyk-Kul is a large mountain lake in the northern Tian Shan of Kyrgyzstan, at about 1,600 meters above sea level, on the routes between the steppe and the oases and near cemeteries whose graves have been linked to an early stage of the Black Death.
facts: Issyk-Kul has an area of about 6,200 square kilometers, a maximum depth of about 668 meters and no outlet; the lake is slightly saline and rarely freezes despite its elevation and cold winters, and its name is usually rendered "warm lake" in Kyrgyz, though the literal meaning is closer to "hot lake."
Saka burial mounds around the lake date from the 1st millennium BCE; the Saka were Iranian-speaking pastoralists related to the Scythians.
Underwater surveys have reported settlement remains and objects from the shallows, dated variously from the Bronze Age to the Middle Ages; interpretations vary.
Routes across the Tian Shan connecting the steppe with the oases of Central Asia passed near the lake.
Gravestones in cemeteries at Kara-Djigach and Burana, in the region of Issyk-Kul, record deaths from pestilence in 1338 to 1339.

A 2022 study reported Yersinia pestis DNA from graves at Kara-Djigach and concluded that the strain was close to the ancestor of the lineage that caused the Black Death; some researchers question whether this locates the origin of the pandemic.
place/issyk-kul.context: Issyk-Kul was used by Saka groups related to the Scythians and lay near routes of the Opening of the Silk Roads. Its region is one candidate for the beginning of the Black Death. It sits in the Iron Age and the region Central Asian Steppe, and belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life, Trade and Economy and Science.
place/issyk-kul.observer: The Observer notes that a community's grief-rites left the evidence that later science used: gravestones that named the cause of death, read six centuries afterward through ancient DNA, an unplanned act of memory-outsourcing that dated the disease's path. A warm, ice-free mountain lake on routes between pastoral and farming societies drew successive peoples, and the same routes carried the pathogen. The origin of the Black Death is still debated, and the reading would weaken if later studies place the pandemic's origin elsewhere.
questions: Did the Black Death begin near Issyk-Kul, or did a plague lineage already circulate more widely?
What do the submerged sites on the lake bed show about earlier settlement?

2026-09-27: The lake has no current outlet (some hydrologists suggest underground filtration), its salinity is approximately 0.6 percent, and despite the elevation and cold winters it rarely freezes. [Wikipedia on Issyk-Kul]

2026-09-27: Graves near Issyk-Kul carried tombstones with Syriac inscriptions giving the name of the deceased, the year of death and often the cause, showing a spike in deaths from pestilence in 1338 to 1339. [Wikipedia on Black Death]

[Wikipedia on Black Death]

place/jack-hills-zircons.title: Jack Hills Zircons
place/jack-hills-zircons.summary: The Jack Hills zircons are tiny crystals from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, some dated to about 4.4 billion years, the oldest known pieces of Earth's crust.
facts: The zircon grains occur in ancient sedimentary rock in the Narryer Terrane of Western Australia, reworked into rocks that are themselves about 3 billion years old.
The oldest grains are dated by uranium-lead decay to roughly 4.4 billion years, only about 150 million years after Earth formed.
Oxygen-isotope ratios in some grains have been interpreted as evidence that their parent magma had interacted with liquid water, though this reading is contested.
The grains survive because zircon is chemically tough and resists weathering and remelting.
No rock of comparable age is known on Earth; the grains are the only direct samples of Hadean crust.
place/jack-hills-zircons.context: The Jack Hills grains give the Hadean Eon its only direct mineral witnesses and are used to argue about when oceans and continental crust first formed. They sit alongside the question of Origin of Life. Jack Hills Zircons sits in the Hadean Eon and the region Oceania, and belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life and Science.
place/jack-hills-zircons.observer: The Observer notes that the planet's earliest testimony consists of a few grains smaller than a pinhead, kept only because they were hard enough to outlast everything around them. What survives is not a fair sample of what existed, a lesson that recurs in every later record.
questions: Did liquid-water oceans exist by 4.3 billion years ago?
How much continental crust existed in the Hadean?

place/jamestown.title: Jamestown
place/jamestown.summary: Jamestown, on the James River in Virginia, USA, was founded in 1607 as the first permanent English settlement in North America and was the capital of the Virginia colony until 1699.
facts: Jamestown was founded in May 1607 by about 105 English men and boys sent by the Virginia Company of London, on land within a paramount chiefdom of many Algonquian-speaking communities led by Wahunsenacawh, whom the English called Powhatan.

In the winter of 1609 to 1610, known as the Starving Time, hunger and disease reduced the colony from a few hundred people (commonly given as about 500) to about 60, and accounts and archaeological evidence record cannibalism.
John Rolfe's tobacco, first harvested successfully in 1614, gave the colony an export crop and increased the colonists' demand for land and labor.

In July 1619 the first representative assembly in English America met at Jamestown; in late August an English privateer, the White Lion, landed about 20 Africans at Point Comfort, downriver, who had been taken from a Portuguese slave ship, and they were traded for food, and some were brought to Jamestown; their legal status is debated.

A Powhatan attack on 22 March 1622 killed more than 300 colonists, about a third of the English population, and years of war followed; Powhatan deaths from war and introduced disease are poorly recorded.
Jamestown was burned in 1676 during Bacon's Rebellion, and the capital moved to Middle Plantation, renamed Williamsburg, in 1699 after the statehouse burned in 1698.
Archaeologists found the remains of the 1607 fort in 1996, after it had long been thought lost to river erosion.
place/jamestown.context: Jamestown was an outpost of the Columbian Exchange in North America, sending tobacco to Europe and receiving people, animals and diseases across the Atlantic, and the arrival of 1619 belongs to the history of the Atlantic Slave Trade. It sits in the Early Modern Period and the region North America, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and War and Conflict.
place/jamestown.observer: The Observer notes that Jamestown is a place where two claims to the same land met, an English company's charter and a Powhatan chiefdom's territory, and that the settlement survived only after it found a crop that turned land and labor into exported wealth. The year 1619 is remembered for a representative assembly and for the arrival of enslaved Africans, and the Observer holds that both belong in one account, with the deaths of colonists, Powhatan people and Africans recorded as suffering. The reading would weaken if new records show that Virginia's system of hereditary slavery grew from later laws with little connection to the 1619 arrivals.
questions: What was the legal status of the Africans landed in 1619, and how did Virginia's law of slavery develop afterward?
How many Powhatan people died from war and introduced disease in the first decades of the colony?

place/jericho.title: Jericho
place/jericho.summary: Jericho, at Tell es-Sultan in the Jordan Valley, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements, with permanent occupation beginning around 9000 BCE.
facts: The site lies in the West Bank, about 250 meters below sea level, near a perennial spring.
Excavations by Kathleen Kenyon in the 1950s found a stone wall and a large stone tower dated to roughly 8000 BCE.
The purpose of the wall, defense against attack or protection from floods and mudflow, is debated.
Houses in the later Pre-Pottery Neolithic B period contained skulls with facial features modeled in plaster, dated to around 7000 BCE.
Jericho is often described as one of the world's oldest towns.
place/jericho.context: Jericho illustrates early sedentary life and stone architecture in the Levant during The Agricultural Revolution, long before the cities of The Urban Revolution in Uruk. Jericho sits in the Neolithic and the region Levant and Anatolia, and belongs to the theme thread of Kinship and Society and Technology.
place/jericho.observer: The Observer notes that a community built a large wall and tower, and also preserved the faces of the dead in plaster, before it had metal or writing. Defense, memory, and grief all seem to have been present at the start of settled life.
questions: Was the wall for defense, flood control, or status display?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Kenyon excavated Tell es-Sultan 1952-58 and found plastered skulls from 1953; site about 250 m below sea level [Durham University on Jericho]

place/jerusalem.title: Jerusalem
place/jerusalem.summary: Jerusalem is a city in the Judean hills of the southern Levant, settled since about the 4th millennium BCE and holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims, whose political status is disputed today.
facts: Settlement on the spur above the Gihon spring dates from about the 4th millennium BCE, and Egyptian Execration Texts of the 19th century BCE and the Amarna letters of the 14th century BCE may contain the earliest mentions of the city, though this is debated.

According to the Hebrew Bible, King David captured the city about 1000 BCE and his son Solomon built the First Temple; archaeologists debate the size of Jerusalem in the 10th century BCE, and the city grew markedly by the 8th century BCE.
Babylonian forces destroyed Jerusalem and the First Temple in 586 BCE and deported part of its population; the Second Temple was dedicated in 516 BCE.

Roman forces destroyed the city and the Second Temple in 70 CE; after the Bar Kokhba revolt (132 to 135 or 136 CE, sources vary on the end year) the Romans refounded it as Aelia Capitolina and barred Jews from entering.

The Church of the Holy Sepulchre was built in the 4th century under Constantine; Muslim forces took the city in 638 (some sources give 637), and the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik completed the Dome of the Rock in 691 to 692.

Crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099 and killed many of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants, with estimates of the dead varying widely; Saladin retook it in 1187, and it was under Ottoman rule from 1517 to 1917.

UNESCO inscribed the Old City of Jerusalem and its walls in 1981. The city was divided between Israel and Jordan in 1948 and has been under Israeli control since 1967, and its status remains disputed between Israelis and Palestinians.
place/jerusalem.context: Jerusalem's history is tied to Babylon through the destruction of 586 BCE, and to the Romans, the Rise of Islam, the Crusades and the Ottoman Empire through later conquests. It sits in the Bronze Age (its earliest settlement) and the region Levant and Anatolia, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief and War and Conflict.
place/jerusalem.observer: The Observer notes that Jerusalem is a place where three meaning-engines, Jewish, Christian and Muslim, locate some of their most significant sites within a few hundred meters of one another, so one spot can hold the claim-lines of several communities, and builders of each period have reused or replaced earlier structures. The city's long record of sieges, destructions and massacres is recorded here as suffering, whichever community was its victim at the time. The reading would weaken if the sanctity of particular sites proves to have been less continuous over time than each tradition holds.

place/karakorum.title: Karakorum
place/karakorum.summary: Karakorum was the capital of the Mongol Empire in the Orkhon Valley of central Mongolia, built from 1235 under Ögedei Khan, and it was damaged and razed by Ming forces in the 1370s and 1380s.
facts: Karakorum stood in the Orkhon Valley; Chinggis Khan is reported to have set up a camp there around 1220, and his son Ögedei ordered a walled city built from 1235.
Craftsmen and captives from conquered lands, including China, Central Asia and Europe, were settled at Karakorum to work as artisans.

William of Rubruck, a Flemish Franciscan sent by Louis IX of France, visited Karakorum in 1254 and described temples of several traditions, mosques, a Christian church, and a silver tree that dispensed drinks, made by the French goldsmith Guillaume Boucher.
After Kublai Khan took power in 1260 and shifted the center of the empire to northern China, Karakorum declined.

Ming forces damaged the city in 1372 and razed it in 1380, and one passage dates the destruction of the permanent palace to 1388; the Buddhist monastery of Erdene Zuu was built nearby from 1585, partly with stone from the ruins.

The ruins of Karakorum were identified in the 19th century and excavated by a Soviet-Mongolian expedition in 1948 and 1949; UNESCO inscribed the Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape, which includes the site, in 2004.
place/karakorum.context: Karakorum was the capital of the Mongol Empire during the period of the Mongol Conquests, in a valley that also holds inscriptions of the earlier Göktürk Khaganate, and it was destroyed by forces of the Ming Dynasty. It sits in the Medieval Period and the region Central Asian Steppe, and belongs to the theme threads of War and Conflict, Trade and Economy and Religion and Belief.
place/karakorum.observer: The Observer notes that Karakorum was a fixed point built by a people whose power rested on mobility, a place to gather tribute, envoys and skilled captives, where the silver tree served as a status-signal aimed at foreign delegations. It was the center of the empire for only a few decades before power moved toward the taxable cities of northern China, which suggests that the capital followed the revenue and not the herds. The forced resettlement of artisans is a reminder that such a capital was built partly through sanctioned harm. The sources, mostly written by outsiders, do not settle how much the city mattered to the Mongol elite compared with the camps they moved between.

How much does Rubruck's account, written by a visiting envoy, reflect the city as its rulers saw it?

place/karnak.title: Karnak
place/karnak.summary: Karnak is a vast temple complex at Thebes, near modern Luxor in Egypt, dedicated mainly to the god Amun-Ra and built and enlarged over about 2,000 years from the Middle Kingdom to the Ptolemaic period.
facts: Karnak's earliest surviving structures date to the reign of Senusret I, around 1970 BCE, and kings added to the complex until the Ptolemaic period.
The Great Hypostyle Hall at Karnak, begun by Seti I and completed by Ramesses II in the 13th century BCE, has 134 columns in 16 rows, the tallest about 21 meters high.
The walls of Karnak carry royal inscriptions, including annals of the campaigns of Thutmose III, reliefs of the Battle of Kadesh, and a relief of the campaign of Shoshenq I in Canaan.
Hatshepsut's obelisk at Karnak stands about 30 meters high; images and inscriptions of Hatshepsut were later removed from many monuments, and the motives are debated.
Papyri of the 12th century BCE record large estates and tens of thousands of dependents attached to the temples of Amun.
Kings of the Kushite 25th Dynasty added to Karnak in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE.

An avenue of sphinxes about 2.7 kilometers long linked Karnak with Luxor Temple, and its restored length was reopened in 2021; UNESCO inscribed Ancient Thebes with its Necropolis, including Karnak, in 1979.
place/karnak.context: Karnak was the religious center of the Ancient Egyptians at Thebes, on the east bank of the Nile River across from the tombs of the Valley of the Kings. Its walls record the Battle of Kadesh, and kings of Kingdom of Kush added to it. Karnak sits in the Bronze Age and the region Nile Valley, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief, Art and Ritual and War and Conflict.
place/karnak.observer: The Observer notes that Karnak works as an accumulating archive in stone: each ruler added buildings and cut his name and campaigns into the walls, so the temple is both a religious site and a public record of royal claims. The removal of Hatshepsut's images shows the claim-line reaching backward, since later rulers could edit the record of a predecessor, which makes the walls an official memory and not a neutral one. A temple holding large estates and dependents also shows a meaning-engine acting as an economic institution. The reading would weaken if the erasures prove to have been less deliberate or less selective than assumed.

How large were the temple's estates at their height?

place/kilwa-kisiwani.title: Kilwa Kisiwani
place/kilwa-kisiwani.summary: Kilwa Kisiwani is an island town off the coast of southern Tanzania that was a leading Swahili port from about the 12th to the 15th century, trading gold from the interior for goods carried across the Indian Ocean.
facts: Kilwa Kisiwani was occupied from about the 9th century CE, and its Great Mosque has an earliest section dated to between 1131 and 1170 (12th century, though local oral tradition places the founding earlier), enlarged in the early 14th century.

The Kilwa Chronicle, written in the 16th century, traces the ruling dynasty to a founder from Shiraz in Persia; archaeological and linguistic evidence indicates that Kilwa's society was rooted in African coastal communities that took part in Indian Ocean trade.

From about the 13th century Kilwa controlled the gold trade from Sofala, in the south, whose gold came from the interior of Zimbabwe, and the town minted its own coins, among the earliest in sub-Saharan Africa.
Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman built the palace and market complex of Husuni Kubwa in the early 14th century.
The traveler Ibn Battuta visited Kilwa in about 1331 and described it as one of the most beautiful and well-constructed towns.
Portuguese forces attacked Kilwa in 1505 and built a fort; the town later came under Omani influence and was involved in the trade in enslaved people in the 18th and 19th centuries.
UNESCO inscribed the Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara in 1981.
place/kilwa-kisiwani.context: Kilwa Kisiwani was one of the Swahili Coast City-States and a hub of the Indian Ocean Trade Network; its gold came through the trade that also supplied Great Zimbabwe's region, and the Portuguese Sea Route to India led to its attack in 1505. It sits in the Medieval Period and the region Sub-Saharan Africa, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, Religion and Belief and Art and Ritual.
place/kilwa-kisiwani.observer: The Observer notes that Kilwa's wealth came from standing between two exchange-webs, the gold of the interior and the ships of the Indian Ocean: the town made none of its main goods but profited from the position between them. The founding story of a Persian origin may have served as a status-signal within a Muslim trading world, while the archaeological evidence shows local African roots, so the story and the record point in different directions. The reading would weaken if excavation shows that Kilwa's wealth depended more on local production than on trade in transit.

place/knossos.title: Knossos
place/knossos.summary: Knossos is an archaeological site near Heraklion on the Greek island of Crete, occupied from about 7000 BCE and the site of the largest palace of the Minoan civilization, built from about 1900 BCE.
facts: Knossos was occupied by farmers by about 7000 BCE, and the first palace was built about 1900 BCE; an earthquake destroyed it about 1700 BCE and a larger palace was built after it.
The palace held storerooms for oil, grain and wine, workshops and frescoes, including bull-leaping scenes, and clay tablets in Linear A, a script that has not been deciphered.
Tablets in Linear B, which was deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952 as an early form of Greek, show that Mycenaean Greeks controlled Knossos by about 1450 BCE.
The palace was destroyed by fire; the date is debated, with proposals from about 1375 to about 1200 BCE.
Arthur Evans excavated Knossos from 1900 and rebuilt parts of it with concrete columns and repainted frescoes; the reconstructions are controversial among archaeologists.
The name "Minoan" is a modern term drawn from the legendary King Minos, and later Greek myth placed the Minotaur and its labyrinth at Knossos; whether the palace inspired the myth is uncertain.
Estimates of the population of Knossos vary widely.
place/knossos.context: Knossos was the largest palace of the Minoans, came under the Mycenaean Greeks, and shaped the memory of the Ancient Greeks; its tablets are central to the story of the Invention of Writing in the Aegean. It sits in the Neolithic (its earliest farming settlement) and the region Mediterranean Basin, and belongs to the theme threads of Art and Ritual, Trade and Economy and Language and Writing.
place/knossos.observer: The Observer notes that Knossos is understood mainly through counting: tablets of stores and allotments show a palace economy that kept records of oil, grain and wine, memory-outsourcing for storage and not for storytelling, while the Minoans' own script remains unread. What visitors see is also an early 20th-century interpretation, since Evans's concrete and paint present a Bronze Age palace through his own ideas of it. The reading would weaken if new work shows that the reconstructions changed the palace's evidence less than critics claim.
questions: What do the Linear A tablets say, and what language do they record?
How did Knossos come under Mycenaean control, and when was it finally destroyed?

place/kolyma.title: Kolyma
place/kolyma.summary: Kolyma is a remote region of northeastern Siberia, Russia, that from 1932 until the 1950s held the Soviet Union's largest system of forced-labor camps, where prisoners mined gold and other metals in extreme cold and many died.
facts: Kolyma lies along the Kolyma River in the far northeast of Siberia, where average winter temperatures run from about minus 19 to minus 38 degrees Celsius, colder still in the interior.

Gold was found on the Kolyma River in the early 20th century, and in 1931 the Soviet state created Dalstroy, a state trust that developed the region with prisoners from the Gulag system, the first of whom arrived in 1932.

Prisoners included people convicted of ordinary crimes and of political offenses, and many were sent during the Great Terror of 1937 to 1938; secret-police records cited by historians put about two million people shipped to the Kolyma camps between 1930 and 1955, with a recorded peak camp population of about 200,000 in 1952.
Estimates of deaths in the Kolyma camps range from about 250,000 to over a million, from hunger, cold, disease, overwork and executions; the full toll is uncertain.
Prisoners built the Kolyma Highway between Magadan and Yakutsk, known as the "Road of Bones" because of the deaths among its builders.
Varlam Shalamov, who was imprisoned in the Kolyma camps, wrote the short stories known as the Kolyma Tales about them.
Dalstroy was dissolved in 1957, and a memorial, the Mask of Sorrow, was unveiled in Magadan in 1996.
place/kolyma.context: Kolyma was a major site of the Gulag under the Soviet state that emerged from the Russian Revolution, in a region that Russia had entered through the Russian Expansion into Siberia. Much of what is known about the camps comes from survivors' writing and from archives opened after the Collapse of the Soviet Union. It sits in the Industrial Age and the region Siberia and the Arctic, and belongs to the theme threads of War and Conflict and Trade and Economy.
place/kolyma.observer: The Observer notes that Kolyma is a case of sanctioned harm carried out through economic administration: prisoners were counted as labor for gold production, and their deaths were entered in ledgers, which the Observer records as suffering. The record of the place comes from two sources that do not always agree, survivors' writing and, after 1991, opened archives, which is why the death toll is given here as a range. The reading would weaken if fuller archival access shows that the camps served aims other than production more than this account suggests.
questions: How many people died in the Kolyma camps, and how many survived?
How is Kolyma remembered inside Russia today?

place/kuk-early-agricultural-site.title: Kuk Early Agricultural Site
place/kuk-early-agricultural-site.summary: The Kuk Early Agricultural Site in the highlands of Papua New Guinea preserves drainage ditches and gardens showing that people cultivated wetlands there for at least 7,000 years.
facts: The site is in the Wahgi Valley of Papua New Guinea and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2008.
It is reported to show agricultural use for at least 7,000 years, possibly beginning as early as 10,000 years ago.
Excavations show a gradual shift from exploiting taro and yam on wetland margins about 7,000 years ago to organized cultivation of bananas on drained ground about 4,000 years ago.
It is one of the few places worldwide widely regarded as an independent center of plant domestication.
The highlands of New Guinea were settled by people descended from those who reached Sahul more than 50,000 years ago.
place/kuk-early-agricultural-site.context: Kuk shows that agriculture arose independently in Oceania, in parallel with The Agricultural Revolution in Southwest Asia and Domestication of Rice in East Asia. Its inhabitants belonged to the population that came through the Peopling of Sahul. Kuk Early Agricultural Site sits in the Neolithic and the region Oceania, and belongs to the theme thread of Technology.
place/kuk-early-agricultural-site.observer: The Observer notes that in this region, farming was developed by people whose ancestors had been in place for tens of thousands of years, undermining the idea that agriculture was a necessary next step for all societies.
questions: Which crops were first cultivated at Kuk, and when?

place/kyoto.title: Kyoto
place/kyoto.summary: Kyoto is a city on the Japanese island of Honshu, founded in 794 CE as the imperial capital Heian-kyō and the seat of the emperor until 1868 to 1869.
facts: Kyoto was founded in 794 by Emperor Kanmu as Heian-kyō, on a grid plan modeled on Chinese capitals such as Chang'an.
Under the Heian court (794 to 1185) Kyoto was the center of court culture, including the novel The Tale of Genji, written in the early 11th century by Murasaki Shikibu.
The Ashikaga shogunate ruled from Kyoto from 1336 to 1573, and the Onin War (1467 to 1477) destroyed much of the city.
Under the Tokugawa shogunate (1603 to 1868) political power lay in Edo, while Kyoto remained the imperial seat and a center of crafts and Buddhist institutions.
The emperor moved to Tokyo (formerly Edo) in 1868 to 1869 after the Meiji Restoration, ending Kyoto's role as capital.
In 1945 Kyoto was removed from the list of possible atomic-bomb targets at the urging of US Secretary of War Henry Stimson, who is traditionally said to have cited its cultural significance.
UNESCO inscribed 17 "Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto" in 1994.
place/kyoto.context: Kyoto's plan followed Chang'an, and the city succeeded Nara as the imperial capital. It remained the imperial seat under the Tokugawa Shogunate and ceased to be the capital with the Meiji Restoration. It sits in the Medieval Period and the region East Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Art and Ritual, Religion and Belief and War and Conflict.
place/kyoto.observer: The Observer notes that Kyoto held an imperial house for more than a thousand years while, for much of that time, armies and administrations answered to shoguns elsewhere, so the story-glue of legitimacy and the practical power to govern sat in different places. A city laid out from a foreign template was maintained through fires and wars as a store of court culture, and its survival in 1945 shows that a city can be spared because of what its buildings hold, in a war that destroyed others. This reading would weaken if the decision not to bomb Kyoto rested mainly on operational reasons and not on cultural ones.
questions: How much of Kyoto's original Heian layout survives in the modern street plan?
How far did cultural reasons, compared with military ones, decide Kyoto's removal from the 1945 target list?

place/l-anse-aux-meadows.title: L'Anse aux Meadows
place/l-anse-aux-meadows.summary: L'Anse aux Meadows is an archaeological site on the northern tip of Newfoundland, Canada, where Norse people from Greenland built a small settlement of sod buildings around 1000 CE, the only widely accepted Norse site in North America.
facts: L'Anse aux Meadows lies at the northernmost tip of Newfoundland; Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad found it in 1960 with the help of a local resident, George Decker, and excavated it in the 1960s.
The site has eight buildings of sod over wooden frames, including an iron smithy, a carpentry workshop and a boat-repair area, and more than 800 Norse objects were found.
Radiocarbon dates place activity between about 990 and 1050 CE; a 2021 study of tree rings, using a solar-storm signal in the year 993, dated felled timber cut with metal tools to 1021 CE.

The occupation was short, perhaps about 20 years, though this is debated, and no burials or signs of farming were found, so the site appears to have been left in an orderly way; the date_end of 1030 is a rough placeholder.
Butternuts found at the site grow farther south, so Norse travelers reached or traded with regions beyond Newfoundland.
The Icelandic sagas, written down in the 13th century, describe voyages to a land called Vinland, and whether L'Anse aux Meadows is that place or a base for voyages farther south is debated.
UNESCO inscribed L'Anse aux Meadows in 1978.
place/l-anse-aux-meadows.context: L'Anse aux Meadows records a voyage by the Norse that reached North America about five centuries before the Columbian Exchange, long after the Peopling of the Americas. It sits in the Medieval Period and the region North America, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and Technology.
place/l-anse-aux-meadows.observer: The Observer notes that here a story-glue, the sagas, and a physical record, the sod buildings and iron working, were long treated as separate until the Ingstads matched them. The site shows a link between two hemispheres that did not become an exchange-web, because no lasting settlement, herds or diseases were left to change either side. The sagas describe meetings with the region's Indigenous people, and how those meetings went is known only from the Norse side. The reading would weaken if evidence shows that contact between the Norse and northeastern peoples was more frequent and lasting than a short-lived camp suggests.

How long was the site occupied, and why was it left?

place/lake-baikal.title: Lake Baikal
place/lake-baikal.summary: Lake Baikal is a rift lake in southern Siberia, Russia, the deepest and oldest lake on Earth and the largest by volume of fresh water, with people living around it for many thousands of years and a UNESCO listing since 1996.
facts: Lake Baikal lies in a rift valley, is about 636 kilometers long, has a maximum depth of 1,642 meters, and holds about 20 percent of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water.
The Baikal rift basin is estimated to be 25 to 30 million years old, which makes the lake the oldest on Earth; this geologic age is far older than any human presence.

More than 1,000 species of plants and 2,500 species of animals have been recorded in and around Lake Baikal, with the true totals thought to be higher; many are found nowhere else, including the Baikal seal, a freshwater seal.
Hunter-fisher-gatherers of the Kitoi culture buried their dead around the lake from about the 5th millennium BCE, and much older Paleolithic sites, such as Mal'ta, lie nearby.
Russian explorers reached Lake Baikal in the 1640s, beginning Russian settlement among the Buryat and Evenki peoples.

A pulp and paper mill on the southern shore discharged waste into the lake from 1966, with production interrupted between 2008 and 2010 before a final closure in 2013, and it was one of the earliest targets of organized environmental protest in the Soviet Union.
UNESCO inscribed Lake Baikal in 1996.
place/lake-baikal.context: Lake Baikal lies near the Paleolithic site linked to Mal'ta and the Ancient North Eurasians, and its shores were reached by the Russian Expansion into Siberia in the 17th century. It sits in the Neolithic (its earliest Holocene burials) and the region Siberia and the Arctic, and belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life and Science.
place/lake-baikal.observer: The Observer notes that Lake Baikal is valued both as a store of an unusual biota and as a resource, that both valuations have shaped policy and the state of the lake, and that the balance between them has shifted with the political era. A lake that took millions of years to form and holds a fifth of the planet's unfrozen fresh water could be altered by one industrial plant within a few decades, which shows the mismatch between geological and human timescales. The reading would weaken if measurements show that the mill's effect on the lake as a whole was small compared with natural variation.
questions: How much lasting change did the pulp mill cause in the lake's ecosystem?
How did people live around Lake Baikal in the Neolithic, and how did they treat their dead?

place/lake-titicaca.title: Lake Titicaca
place/lake-titicaca.summary: Lake Titicaca is a large high-altitude lake on the border of Peru and Bolivia, sacred to the Inca as the birthplace of their first rulers and long settled by farming and fishing communities of the Andean highlands.
facts: The lake lies at about 3,812 meters elevation, with a surface area of about 8,372 square kilometers, and is often called the world's highest navigable lake for commercial craft.

Communities around the lake farmed and fished from at least the mid-2nd millennium BCE; the date_start of -1500 marks the period conventionally associated with early settled use of the basin, and older human presence in the Andes belongs to a different brief.
The Tiwanaku civilization, centered south of the lake, built a temple on the Island of the Moon by about 650 to 1000 CE and left pottery and stonework recovered from the islands.

Inca tradition holds that the first Inca ruler, Manco Cápac, and his sister-wife Mama Ocllo, emerged from the lake or its Island of the Sun by order of the sun god Inti; the Sacred Rock on the Island of the Sun is linked in tradition to Manco Cápac's remains.
The Uros people build and live on floating islands made from layers of totora reed; about 1,200 Uros lived on some 60 such islands as of 2011.

A 2011 United Nations report found high concentrations of cadmium, arsenic and lead in parts of the lake, and its water level fell 81 centimeters between April and November 2009, attributed to shorter rainy seasons and glacier melt in its tributaries.
place/lake-titicaca.context: Lake Titicaca is the traditional birthplace of the ruling line of the Inca Empire, whose later capital was Cusco. It sits in the Bronze Age by the date_start used here and the region Andes, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief and Earth Systems and Life.
place/lake-titicaca.observer: The Observer notes that a body of water this large and this high became a meaning-engine's point of origin: the Inca placed their ruling ancestors' arrival at the lake's islands, tying a kin-lattice claim to a landscape rather than to a single city. The Uros islands are themselves a technology, floating ground built and rebuilt from reed, which the Observer reads as a claim-line drawn on water rather than land. The reading would weaken if the Manco Cápac tradition is shown to be a later invention with little connection to how the earliest lake communities saw their own origins.
questions: How far back does continuous human use of the Titicaca basin go, and what shaped its earliest settlement?
How much of the lake's current pollution and water-level decline is reversible?

place/library-of-alexandria.title: Library of Alexandria
place/library-of-alexandria.summary: The Library of Alexandria was a major research library in Ptolemaic Egypt, founded in the early 3rd century BCE as part of the Mouseion, and its decline was gradual rather than a single catastrophe.
facts: It was founded under the first Ptolemaic rulers, in the 3rd century BCE.
Scholars associated with it include Eratosthenes, who estimated the circumference of the Earth, and Callimachus, who compiled a catalog of works.
Euclid is traditionally said to have worked in Alexandria, though details of his life are uncertain.
Julius Caesar's fire in 48 BCE damaged some holdings, but the institution continued.
Its decline resulted from reduced funding, political upheaval, and the loss of scholars over several centuries.
place/library-of-alexandria.context: The library grew from the conquests of Alexander the Great and inherited the tradition of Aristotle. Its later scholars include Hypatia. Library of Alexandria sits in the Classical Antiquity and the region Nile Valley, and belongs to the theme thread of Science and Language and Writing.
place/library-of-alexandria.observer: The Observer notes that the popular story of a single great burning is easier to remember than the truth of slow neglect. Memory institutions seem to fail more often through budget cuts than through fire.
questions: What was the actual size of the collection?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Founded in the 3rd century BCE under the early Ptolemies; Eratosthenes and Callimachus associated; decline was gradual, with a possible fire in 48 BCE [World History Encyclopedia on the Library of Alexandria]

place/london.title: London
place/london.summary: London is the capital of the United Kingdom, on the Thames River, founded as the Roman town of Londinium in about 47 CE and grown into a leading center of trade, finance and empire and, in the 19th century, the largest city in the world.
facts: Londinium was founded by the Romans in about 47 CE near a crossing of the Thames; Boudica's revolt destroyed it in 60 or 61, and it grew into the largest town in Roman Britain, though clear evidence that it was ever formally the province's capital is lacking, until Roman rule ended around 410.
William I was crowned at Westminster in 1066 and began the Tower of London in about 1078.

The Black Death of 1348 to 1349 killed a large share of London's people, and the Great Plague of 1665 killed tens of thousands; the Great Fire of 1666 destroyed about 13,000 houses and 87 parish churches.
London was probably the largest city in the world from the 1830s to the 1920s, and the world's first underground railway opened there in 1863.
During the 1854 cholera outbreak in Soho, John Snow mapped deaths by address and linked them to a water pump; the "Great Stink" of 1858 led to the building of a sewer system by Joseph Bazalgette.
London was a major center of shipping, insurance and finance for the Atlantic slave trade and for British colonial trade, and the capital of the British Empire.
The German air raids of 1940 to 1941 killed about 20,000 Londoners or more.
place/london.context: London began as a town of the Romans, lost people to the Black Death, grew with the Industrial Revolution, served as the imperial center of the British Raj and other territories, and was bombed in World War II. It sits in Classical Antiquity and the region Europe, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, Science and War and Conflict.
place/london.observer: The Observer notes that London was founded as a bridge town for a foreign state's administration and grew into a hub of an exchange-web that spanned oceans, and that its wealth included profits from the sale and transport of enslaved people, which the Observer records as suffering. The Snow map of 1854 shows a city becoming an object of pattern-taming: tabulating deaths by address led to the identification of a source of disease, a method later used across public health. The reading would weaken if the record shows that London's global role rested more on later trade than on the earlier ones it emphasizes.
questions: How large was Roman Londinium, and why was it abandoned in the 5th century?
How much of London's wealth in the 17th and 18th centuries came from the Atlantic slave trade and related finance?

place/machu-picchu.title: Machu Picchu
place/machu-picchu.summary: Machu Picchu is a stone citadel built about 1450 in the Peruvian Andes, probably as a royal estate for the Inca ruler Pachacuti.
facts: It sits at about 2,430 meters above sea level.
It was abandoned around the time of the Spanish conquest.
Local people knew of it; Hiram Bingham brought it to international attention in 1911.
It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.
place/machu-picchu.context: The site belongs to the Inca Empire. See Andes.
place/machu-picchu.observer: The Observer notes the engineering of terraces and drainage, and the way a ruler's retreat was built at the edge of what is buildable.

place/marajo-island.title: Marajó Island
place/marajo-island.summary: Marajó Island, at the mouth of the Amazon River in Pará, Brazil, was home to the Marajoara culture, which built earthen mounds and made elaborate pottery from about 400 BCE until its decline after European contact in the 16th century.
facts: Marajó, with a land area of about 40,100 square kilometers, is the second-largest island in South America, comparable in size to Switzerland.

The Marajoara culture existed from about 400 BCE to around 1600 CE; people lived in houses with tamped-earth floors, organized in matrilineal clans, and made large ceremonial pottery, including burial urns.

Archaeologist Betty Meggers argued the culture was founded by migrants from the Andes and declined from about 1400 due to poor soil; Anna Roosevelt's later research argued instead that Marajoara society developed independently in the Amazon, with intensive farming and large-scale earthworks, and estimated a peak population of more than 100,000.
European contact in the 16th century brought epidemic disease, and an estimated 90 percent of the island's Indigenous population died from introduced illnesses to which they had no immunity.
The island's economy today rests partly on introduced water buffalo, whose herds, numbering about 450,000, outnumber the roughly 400,000 human residents; lumber and açaí palm are also produced there.
place/marajo-island.context: Marajó Island's builders are the Marajoara Culture, part of the wider evidence gathered under Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths for complex pre-Columbian societies in the Amazon River basin; its population collapse followed the Columbian Exchange. It sits in the Iron Age and the region Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands, and belongs to the theme threads of Kinship and Society and Art and Ritual.
place/marajo-island.observer: The Observer notes that two readings of Marajó, one crediting outside migrants and environmental limits, the other crediting an independent and well-organized society, disagreed less about the pottery and mounds themselves than about how much complexity to expect from a society outside the usual centers of early states, an assumption the Observer treats as itself worth questioning. The population's near-collapse after contact is recorded here as suffering on a scale that removed most of the people who could have explained their own society firsthand, which is part of why the debate persisted so long. The reading would weaken if further excavation shows population and organization closer to Meggers's lower estimates.
questions: How large and how socially organized was Marajoara society at its peak, and how much did later scholars' assumptions about the Amazon shape earlier estimates?
How much of the culture's own memory of itself was lost in the population collapse after contact?

place/marib.title: Marib
place/marib.summary: Marib is a city in Yemen on the edge of the Ramlat al-Sabatayn desert, east of Sanaa, which was the capital of the Kingdom of Saba from about the 8th century BCE and the site of a great dam that irrigated the oasis.
facts: Marib appears in Sabaean inscriptions from about the 8th century BCE and was the capital of the Kingdom of Saba, whose wealth came from the incense trade.

The Great Dam of Marib, first built in about the 8th century BCE, diverted seasonal floods from Wadi Adhanah into irrigation canals and was raised and repaired over many centuries; an inscription records a repair in 542 to 543 CE.
The dam failed for the last time around the 6th century CE; the Quran refers to a flood that ended the prosperity of Saba, which tradition connects with the dam.
Marib has temples of Almaqah, the chief god of Saba, including the oval Awwam temple, which local tradition calls Mahram Bilqis.
A modern dam at Marib, built in the 1980s with funding from the United Arab Emirates, replaced the ancient system.
Since 2015 Marib has been a frontline city in the Yemeni civil war and has taken in large numbers of people displaced by the fighting.
place/marib.context: Marib was the capital of the Kingdom of Saba and a node of the Incense Trade; the failure of its dam is remembered in traditions that entered the sources of the Rise of Islam. It sits in the Iron Age and the region Arabian Peninsula, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, Technology and Religion and Belief.
place/marib.observer: The Observer notes that Marib shows a state built on water as much as on incense: a dam that turned flood into farmland needed labor, tribute and coordination, and the inscribed repairs show that upkeep was a recurring political act. When order failed, so did the dam, which suggests that infrastructure and authority rise and fall together. The later story linking the dam's failure to a moral cause is a story-glue about the fall of a prosperous society. Historians debate whether the dam's collapse caused the decline or reflected a decline already under way, and the reading would weaken if the dam's failures are shown to be mainly hydrological.
questions: When was the first dam built, and how large was the irrigated area?
Did the failure of the dam cause the decline of Marib, or follow it?

place/mausoleum-of-qin-shi-huang.title: Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang
place/mausoleum-of-qin-shi-huang.summary: The Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang is the burial complex of the first emperor of unified China, near Xi'an in Shaanxi, begun in 246 BCE and known for the Terracotta Army of clay soldiers buried in pits east of the tomb mound.
facts: Construction of the Mausoleum began in 246 BCE, when Ying Zheng became king of Qin; he took the title Qin Shi Huang ("First Emperor") after unifying China in 221 BCE and died in 210 BCE.
Sima Qian, writing about a century later, reports that 700,000 laborers worked on the tomb and palace, a figure that cannot be verified.

Farmers digging a well found the Terracotta Army in 1974. The pits hold life-size clay soldiers, horses, chariots and bronze weapons, estimated at about 8,000 figures in total, of which more than 2,000 have been excavated.
The figures were assembled from molded parts, finished by hand and originally painted in bright colors, which mostly faded after exposure to air.
Other pits hold figures of officials, acrobats and musicians, and bronze waterbirds.
The burial mound has not been excavated; soil around it has elevated mercury levels, consistent with Sima Qian's account of mercury in the tomb.
Sima Qian also reports that childless women of the palace and workers who knew the tomb's secrets were sealed inside after the burial; archaeology has not confirmed this account.
UNESCO inscribed the Mausoleum in 1987.
place/mausoleum-of-qin-shi-huang.context: The Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang belongs to the emperor who carried out the Unification of China under Qin and linked walls that became part of the Great Wall of China; the Han Dynasty followed the Qin. It sits in Classical Antiquity and the region East Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of War and Conflict, Art and Ritual and Religion and Belief.
place/mausoleum-of-qin-shi-huang.observer: The Observer notes that a state that standardized script, weights and measures also produced its afterlife army from standardized parts, so a grief-rite and a status-signal were built with the same logic as the state's administration. The labor behind it, reported by Sima Qian in the hundreds of thousands, is a cost to record as suffering, though the figure is uncertain. The reading rests on the modular construction that excavators have documented for the warriors; it would weaken if the unopened tomb proves to differ sharply from the pits.
questions: What does the central tomb chamber contain, and can it be opened without damage?
How many people worked on the mausoleum, and under what conditions?

place/mecca.title: Mecca
place/mecca.summary: Mecca is a city in the Hejaz region of western Saudi Arabia, about 70 kilometers inland from the Red Sea, the birthplace of Muhammad and the holiest city of Islam, whose sanctuary around the Kaaba is the destination of the annual Hajj pilgrimage.
facts: The date of Mecca's first settlement is unknown, and the identification of Mecca with the place Macoraba in Ptolemy's 2nd-century geography is disputed. Muslim sources written after Muhammad's time describe a sanctuary town governed by the Quraysh in the century before Islam.
Islamic tradition places Muhammad's birth in Mecca about 570 CE, his move to Medina in 622, and Mecca's passing under Muslim control in 630 with little fighting.
The Hajj is one of the Five Pillars of Islam, required once in a lifetime of Muslims able to make the journey; Saudi authorities have reported annual attendance in the low millions in recent decades.
Historians disagree about Mecca's importance in long-distance trade before Islam; some describe it as a regional sanctuary and market town rather than a hub of the incense and spice trades.
Mecca was ruled locally by the Sharifs under successive overlords, including the Ottomans from 1517, until the Saudi conquest of 1924 to 1925. Non-Muslims are barred from entering the city.
In the crush at Mina, near Mecca, during the 2015 Hajj, the Saudi authorities reported 769 deaths, while counts compiled from other governments' figures exceeded 2,000.
place/mecca.context: Mecca is the central place of the Rise of Islam, the destination of the Hijra from Medina, and a stop in the peninsula's wider Incense Trade setting. It came under the Umayyad Caliphate and later the Ottoman Empire, and pilgrims came from far away, including the ruler of the Mali Empire, Mansa Musa, who made the Hajj in 1324. Mecca sits in the Medieval Period and the region Arabian Peninsula, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief and Trade and Economy.
place/mecca.observer: The Observer notes that Mecca is a place where a meaning-engine draws millions of strangers to one point each year, creating a recurring exchange-web of people, goods and news that reached from West Africa to Southeast Asia. Pilgrims wear plain white garments (for men, two unstitched cloths), which reduces visible differences of rank during the rites. Pilgrims themselves describe the journey as an act of obedience and devotion, and this reading of its social effects is meant to sit beside that account, not replace it. Crowd disasters such as Mina in 2015 are a recurring cost of gathering at this scale and are recorded here as suffering. The reading would weaken if pilgrim networks turn out to have carried little trade or news compared with their devotional purpose.
questions: What does archaeology show about pre-Islamic Mecca, given how little excavation has been done in the sacred precinct?
How large was Mecca's role in long-distance trade before Islam?

place/medina.title: Medina
place/medina.summary: Medina is a city in the Hejaz region of western Saudi Arabia, known before Islam as Yathrib, to which Muhammad migrated in 622 CE and where he is buried; it is the second holiest city of Islam.
facts: Medina was an oasis settlement called Yathrib before Islam, inhabited by Arab tribes, chiefly the Aws and Khazraj, and by Jewish tribes; its earlier history is poorly documented.
Muhammad and his followers migrated there from Mecca in 622 (the Hijra), the year from which the Islamic calendar counts; Muhammad died and was buried there in 632.
The Constitution of Medina, a document preserved in later sources, sets out obligations among Muslim, Jewish and other groups; its date and authenticity are debated.

Traditional Islamic sources report that two Jewish tribes, Banu Qaynuqa and Banu Nadir, were expelled from Medina, and that the men of a third, Banu Qurayza, were executed in 627, with figures reported from about 400 to 900; some modern historians question details of these accounts.
Medina was the capital of the first caliphs until 656, when Ali moved to Kufa; the Umayyad caliphs later ruled from Damascus.

The Prophet's Mosque in Medina, first built in 622, was enlarged by the Umayyad caliph al-Walid I in the early 8th century and repeatedly since; non-Muslims are barred from the central sanctuary area.
place/medina.context: Medina was the destination of the Hijra from Mecca and the first capital of the Rise of Islam, before rule passed to the Umayyad Caliphate. It sits in the Medieval Period and the region Arabian Peninsula, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief, War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
place/medina.observer: The Observer notes that Medina is where a small community became a polity, and that its founding document, if early, tried to bind kin groups into one order with shared rules for settling disputes, a case of story-glue in the form of law. The same tradition records that defining who belonged also defined who did not, with exile and killing recorded as suffering for the tribes that fell outside. The reading depends on the early dating of the Constitution and on the reliability of sources written generations later, both of which specialists debate.
questions: How early is the Constitution of Medina, and how reliable are the later accounts that preserve it?
What does archaeology show about Yathrib before 622?

place/mekong-river.title: Mekong River
place/mekong-river.summary: The Mekong River is a river of Asia with an estimated length of about 4,900 kilometers, rising on the Tibetan Plateau and flowing through China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam, whose annual flood supports rice farming and one of the world's largest inland fisheries.
facts: The Mekong rises on the Tibetan Plateau and flows through China, along the borders of Myanmar, Laos and Thailand, and through Cambodia and Vietnam into the South China Sea, where it forms a large delta.

Settlement along the Mekong is documented from at least 210 BCE, and the early port of Oc Eo in the delta, part of the state called Funan, traded from about the 1st century CE; the region's much earlier prehistory is not well fixed by the sources consulted here.

The Tonlé Sap, a lake in Cambodia joined to the Mekong, changes its direction of flow with the season: floodwater flows into it in the wet season and back out in the dry season, supporting a major fishery.
The lower basin has about 60 million people, and the river is among the world's most productive inland fisheries.
A French exploration commission in 1866 to 1868 found that rapids made the Mekong unnavigable as a route to China, and the Mekong Delta was a major area of fighting in the Vietnam War.

China has built a cascade of dams on the upper Mekong since the 1990s, and Laos began operating the Xayaburi dam on the lower river in 2019; the Mekong River Commission, formed in 1995, coordinates the lower-basin countries, and the effects of the dams on fish, sediment and flood timing are debated.
place/mekong-river.context: The Mekong River was the corridor of the Khmer Empire and its capital Angkor, and its delta was a theater of the Cold War. It sits in Classical Antiquity (its earliest documented settlement) and the region Southeast Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life, Trade and Economy and Technology.
place/mekong-river.observer: The Observer notes that the Mekong is a river whose annual pulse feeds fish and rice for tens of millions, and that dams upstream change that pulse for people downstream, a relation in which those who control the flow can alter conditions for others across claim-lines that the river itself ignores. The reversing flow of the Tonlé Sap shows a natural rhythm that a whole society organized its seasons around. The reading would weaken if measurements show that the dams' net effect on downstream fish and sediment is smaller than the models suggest.
questions: How much have upstream dams changed the flood pulse, fish migration and delta sediment?
How did early states such as Funan use the river for trade?

place/merv.title: Merv
place/merv.summary: Merv was a major oasis city on the Silk Roads in what is now Turkmenistan, a city of the Achaemenid Persians, a capital of the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun and of the Seljuk sultans, and sacked by the Mongols in 1221.
facts: Merv lies in the Murghab delta oasis near the modern city of Mary; Bronze Age towns of the region, such as Gonur Depe, date to about 2000 BCE, and the walled city of Erk Kala dates from the Achaemenid period, from about the 7th century BCE.
Arab forces took Merv in 651, after the last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, was killed near it.

Abu Muslim launched the Abbasid Revolution from Merv in 747 and declared the new Abbasid dynasty there in February 748; the caliph al-Ma'mun ruled from Merv from about 813 to 818 before moving to Baghdad.
Merv was a Seljuk capital, notably under Sultan Sanjar (reigned 1118 to 1157), whose mausoleum survives, and some estimates suggest it was among the largest cities in the world in the 12th century.
The geographer Yaqut, who studied in Merv's libraries in the early 13th century, described them.

The Mongol army took Merv in 1221; Persian chronicles report hundreds of thousands to over a million killed, figures that modern historians regard as greatly exaggerated but that reflect a severe massacre and destruction.
Merv was rebuilt on a smaller scale in the 15th century and was finally abandoned in the late 18th century.
UNESCO inscribed Ancient Merv in 1999.
place/merv.context: Merv was a satrapy center of the Achaemenid Persians, the political base of the Abbasid Caliphate at its start, and a victim of the Mongol Conquests. It lay on the routes of the Opening of the Silk Roads. Merv sits in Classical Antiquity and the region Central Asian Oases, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, War and Conflict and Science.
place/merv.observer: The Observer notes that Merv's fortunes followed the claim-lines drawn by others: an irrigated oasis city depends on which empire's exchange-web runs through it, and Achaemenids, Seleucids, Arabs, Seljuks and Mongols each held it. The events of 1221 show that a city, unlike a mobile camp, cannot leave, and the reported loss of its libraries suggests that a city's stored writing is as exposed as its people, though those reports are hard to verify. The reading would weaken if the true death toll and the extent of the library losses prove much smaller than the chronicles say.
questions: How many people lived in Merv at its 12th-century peak, and how many died in 1221?
What did Merv's libraries hold, and what happened to them?

place/mesa-verde.title: Mesa Verde
place/mesa-verde.summary: Mesa Verde is a plateau in the Four Corners region of southwestern Colorado, USA, where Ancestral Puebloan farmers lived from about 550 CE until about 1300 and built the cliff dwellings of the late 12th and 13th centuries.
facts: Mesa Verde lies in Montezuma County, Colorado; people used the area for thousands of years before farming communities settled the mesa, and they lived there continuously for about 700 years until the late 13th century.

By the end of the 12th century residents began building cliff dwellings in sandstone alcoves beneath the mesa rim; the park holds more than 5,000 archaeological sites, including about 600 cliff dwellings, and Cliff Palace is among the largest cliff dwellings in North America.
Tree-ring records show a severe drought from 1276 to 1299, and drought, resource depletion and overpopulation are all proposed as causes of instability; the last residents left by about 1300.
Pueblo peoples such as the Hopi, Zuni and Acoma regard the Ancestral Puebloans as their ancestors, and many Pueblo people prefer "Ancestral Puebloan" to the older term "Anasazi".
The ranchers Richard Wetherill and Charlie Mason reached Cliff Palace on 18 December 1888, artifact collecting followed, and the site was protected as a national park in 1906.
UNESCO inscribed Mesa Verde in 1978.
place/mesa-verde.context: Mesa Verde followed the peak of Chaco Canyon, whose great houses declined in the 12th century, and it was contemporary with Cahokia in the Mississippi valley. It sits in the Medieval Period and the region North America, and belongs to the theme threads of Kinship and Society and Earth Systems and Life.
place/mesa-verde.observer: The Observer notes that a place called "abandoned" in one telling is "left" in another: the people who built the cliff dwellings did not vanish, and their descendants keep the memory of the move in sound-code and in place rather than in a mark-code. Building homes in alcoves and leaving them within about a century shows a community adjusting to a drying climate, and the Observer records the leaving as a choice made under hunger and strain. The reading would weaken if the dwellings prove to have served mainly as seasonal storage or ritual sites instead of homes.
questions: Why did residents build in the alcoves after centuries of living on the mesa top, and how much was defense against conflict?
Where did the people who left go, and how did they shape the later Pueblo communities of the Rio Grande?
