place/mexico-city.title: Mexico City
place/mexico-city.summary: Mexico City is the capital of Mexico, built by the Spanish after 1521 on the site of Tenochtitlan in the former Lake Texcoco, and today one of the largest cities in the Americas.
facts: Mexico City was rebuilt by the Spanish on the ruins of Tenochtitlan after the conquest of 1521, with a municipality founded in 1524 as México Tenochtitlán, and it became the capital of the Viceroyalty of New Spain, established in 1535.

The Metropolitan Cathedral, begun in the 1570s and completed in 1813, stands beside the main square, and the buried Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan was uncovered in excavations after workers found the Coyolxauhqui stone in 1978.

The lakes were drained by canals and tunnels from the 17th century in response to floods, and the city now covers much of the old lakebed; parts of it have sunk as much as nine meters and some areas still sink by nearly 50 centimeters a year.
Silver and goods moved through the capital in the Spanish trade system, and the Manila galleons linked New Spain to Asia through the Pacific port of Acapulco.
Mexican independence was secured in September 1821, with Mexico City as the capital of the new state.

The soft lakebed amplifies earthquakes: the quake of 19 September 1985 (magnitude about 8) killed about 10,000 people by official counts, with some estimates several times higher, and the quake of 19 September 2017 (magnitude 7.1) killed more than 300.
The 2020 census counted 9,209,944 people in Mexico City and 21,804,515 in Greater Mexico City, and UNESCO inscribed the Historic Centre and Xochimilco in 1987.
place/mexico-city.context: Mexico City succeeded Tenochtitlan after the Spanish Conquest of the Aztec Empire, and it was a hub of the Columbian Exchange and the Manila Galleon Trade. It was the capital when independence came in the Latin American Wars of Independence. It sits in the Early Modern Period and the region Mesoamerica, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, War and Conflict and Earth Systems and Life.
place/mexico-city.observer: The Observer notes that Mexico City is a capital built directly on an earlier capital, with the Spanish cathedral and plaza placed near the old temple precinct, one claim-line drawn over another, and that the pull of the earlier city's site, its ancestor-weight, shaped the choice. The Mexica lived on the lake through causeways and chinampas, while the modern city sinks into the drained lakebed and is managed by pumping and drainage, so a site chosen for power carries its hazards into later centuries. The reading would weaken if records show that the Spanish chose the site mainly for practical reasons of labor and roads and not for its symbolic value.
questions: How much of Tenochtitlan's street plan and canal system survives beneath the historic center?
How are earthquakes and subsidence changing where and how people live on the old lakebed?

place/mogao-caves.title: Mogao Caves
place/mogao-caves.summary: The Mogao Caves are a complex of Buddhist cave temples cut into a cliff near Dunhuang, in Gansu, China, begun by tradition in 366 CE and decorated with murals and sculptures over about a thousand years at a crossroads of the Silk Roads.
facts: The Mogao Caves lie near the oasis of Dunhuang at the edge of the desert, where Silk Road routes met; Han China had established a commandery at Dunhuang in the late 2nd century BCE.

By tradition the first cave was dug in 366 CE by the monk Yuezun, and work continued into the 14th century; the site has roughly 735 caves (487 known since the early 1900s plus 248 more found between 1988 and 1995), several hundred of which hold murals or painted sculptures, with murals covering about 46,000 square meters.
The art shows Indian, Central Asian and Chinese influences, and donors, including officials, merchants and local rulers, are painted into many caves.
Dunhuang was under Tibetan rule from about 787 to 848, was governed by a local regime from 848, and passed to the Tangut state of Western Xia in about 1036.

The "Library Cave" (Cave 17), sealed around the early 11th century, was opened in 1900 by Wang Yuanlu, a Daoist priest who guarded the caves; it held tens of thousands of manuscripts in Chinese, Tibetan, Sanskrit, Sogdian, Khotanese and other languages, including a printed Diamond Sutra dated 868.

Aurel Stein in 1907, Paul Pelliot in 1908 and others obtained large numbers of these manuscripts, now held in London, Paris and elsewhere; the removals are described in China as theft and by the acquiring institutions as purchases.
UNESCO inscribed the Mogao Caves in 1987, and the Dunhuang Academy has conserved them since 1944.
place/mogao-caves.context: The Mogao Caves grew with the trade of the Opening of the Silk Roads, under the Han Dynasty and the Tang Dynasty, and held documents written by Sogdians and others. They sit in Classical Antiquity and the region East Asia, and belong to the theme threads of Religion and Belief, Art and Ritual and Language and Writing.
place/mogao-caves.observer: The Observer notes that the record of a caravan crossroads survived because a room was sealed: contracts, letters, school exercises and Buddhist texts in many scripts, kept by dry air, a rare case of memory-outsourcing that preserved ordinary life and not only palace records. Donors painted into the murals beside sacred figures joined status-signal and devotion in one image. The scattering of the manuscripts across several countries shows how the record of one place can become the property of many claim-lines. The reason the room was sealed is debated, and the reading would weaken if it proves to have been routine disposal of worn-out texts and not a deliberate act of preservation.
questions: Why was the Library Cave sealed, and by whom?
How should the manuscripts taken from the Mogao Caves be held and shared today?

place/mohenjo-daro.title: Mohenjo-daro
place/mohenjo-daro.summary: Mohenjo-daro was a major city of the Indus Valley Civilization in present-day Pakistan, occupied from about 2500 to 1900 BCE.
facts: It had a grid layout with brick-lined drains and wells.
The 'Great Bath' is a large water tank at the center of its citadel.
It may have held tens of thousands of people.
It was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980.
place/mohenjo-daro.context: Mohenjo-daro is a key site of the Indus Valley Civilization and shows how The Urban Revolution occurred in more than one region.
place/mohenjo-daro.observer: The Observer notes a city with sophisticated sanitation and few weapons or grand tombs. It suggests other ways of organizing a city than the ones best known from Mesopotamia and Egypt.
questions: How was the city governed?

place/monte-alban.title: Monte Alban
place/monte-alban.summary: Monte Alban was the hilltop capital of the Zapotec people in the Oaxaca Valley of Mexico, founded around 500 BCE and abandoned by about 800 CE.
facts: The site sits on a leveled mountaintop overlooking three valleys.
Carved stones known as Danzantes, dated to the early centuries of the city, show figures with glyphs, part of an early Mesoamerican writing tradition.
The city grew to a population of well over ten thousand in its Classic period.
It maintained relations with Teotihuacan, and depictions at Teotihuacan show Zapotec visitors.
It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1987.
place/monte-alban.context: Monte Alban was a major political center of Mesoamerica in the period between the Olmecs and Teotihuacan, and one of the birthplaces of Invention of Writing in the region. Monte Alban sits in the Classical Antiquity and the region Mesoamerica, and belongs to the theme thread of Language and Writing and Religion and Belief.
place/monte-alban.observer: The Observer notes that a city was placed on a mountaintop that had to be leveled by hand and supplied with water from far below. A capital sited for defense and display rather than convenience says something about what its founders valued.
questions: Are the Danzantes true writing?

place/monte-verde.title: Monte Verde
place/monte-verde.summary: Monte Verde is an archaeological site in southern Chile that, for decades, was considered the best evidence that people lived in South America about 14,500 years ago, before the Clovis culture of North America; its age is now debated.
facts: Excavations led by Tom Dillehay from the 1970s exposed wooden hut foundations, leather, rope, and plant remains preserved in a peat bog.
In 1997 a panel of archaeologists inspected the site and accepted an age of about 14,500 years.
The site helped overturn the 'Clovis-first' model; see Peopling of the Americas.
A recent study has proposed a much younger age for the site; specialists dispute this, and the question is unsettled.
place/monte-verde.context: Monte Verde is a key site for the Peopling of the Americas, dating from the end of the Last Glacial Maximum.
place/monte-verde.observer: The Observer notes that a site's importance can outrun its certainty. A single set of dates can hold up a large theory, and the theory is only as strong as the dates.
questions: How old is Monte Verde?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Traditional age about 14,500 years (1997 panel); a recent study proposing a much younger age is disputed [Science News on the Monte Verde Age Debate]

place/nalanda.title: Nalanda
place/nalanda.summary: Nalanda is an archaeological site in Bihar, India, of a Buddhist monastic university founded in about the 5th century CE that drew students from across Asia until it was sacked around 1200.
facts: Nalanda was founded in about the 5th century CE, traditionally under the Gupta ruler Kumaragupta I, and grew into a large monastic university.
The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang studied at Nalanda in the 630s and 640s and reported about 10,000 residents; another Chinese pilgrim, Yijing, described it in 675.
Students and visitors came from China, Tibet, Korea, Central Asia and Southeast Asia, and in the 9th century a ruler of Srivijaya funded a monastery at Nalanda.
Nalanda taught Buddhist philosophy, logic, grammar and medicine.

Forces under Bakhtiyar Khalji sacked Nalanda around 1200; later traditions say its library burned for months, and historians debate how completely it was destroyed and whether its decline began earlier.
UNESCO inscribed the Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara in 2016, and a new Nalanda University opened in 2014.
place/nalanda.context: Nalanda was founded under the Gupta Empire, was visited by pilgrims from the Tang Dynasty and supported by rulers of Srivijaya, and it fell during the raids that preceded the Delhi Sultanate. It sits in Classical Antiquity and the region South Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Science, Religion and Belief and Language and Writing.
place/nalanda.observer: The Observer notes that Nalanda concentrated teachers, texts and students from across Asia, an exchange-web of ideas in which monks carried texts and methods to China and Tibet, a case of memory-outsourcing in an institution and not in a single book. Its loss around 1200 shows that a store of knowledge depends on the institution that keeps it, and that the loss of an institution can be slower and less dramatic than later traditions of one great fire suggest. The reading would weaken if new evidence shows that Nalanda's decline was mainly the result of reduced patronage before its sack.
questions: How much of Nalanda's decline came before the sack of around 1200?
How large was the library, and what did it hold?

place/nan-madol.title: Nan Madol
place/nan-madol.summary: Nan Madol is a ruined city of artificial stone islets built in a lagoon off Pohnpei, in the Federated States of Micronesia, the ceremonial and political center of the Saudeleur dynasty from about the 12th century until around 1628.
facts: Nan Madol consists of about 92 artificial islets built from stacked basalt columns and coral fill, linked by tidal canals, over a core area of about 1.5 by 0.5 kilometers.

Human activity at the site dates from as early as the 1st or 2nd century CE, islet construction began in the 8th or 9th century, and the megalithic stonework that gives the site its present form was built from about 1180 to 1200.

Tradition holds that the Saudeleur dynasty ruled Pohnpei from Nan Madol, uniting an estimated population of about 25,000 on the island, though the number of people living at Nan Madol itself was probably under 1,000.
Around 1628 a warrior named Isokelekel is said in tradition to have invaded and ended Saudeleur rule; some scholars also point to population decline as a contributing cause of the site's abandonment.
UNESCO inscribed Nan Madol as a World Heritage Site in 2016.
place/nan-madol.context: Nan Madol's builders were part of the wider settlement of the Pacific carried by the Austronesian Expansion and the Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific, and Micronesian voyaging traditions share roots with cultures such as the Lapita Culture farther south and east. It sits in the Medieval Period and the region Oceania, and belongs to the theme threads of Kinship and Society and Technology.
place/nan-madol.observer: The Observer notes that Nan Madol turned a lagoon into a claim-line: a ruling lineage built its seat on stone islets separated from the rest of the island by water, a status-signal that set the center of power physically apart from those it ruled. The tradition of Isokelekel's conquest, like many founding and ending stories, is ancestor-weight carried forward by the community rather than a document, and the Observer treats it as a claim to be tested rather than a settled fact. The reading would weaken if archaeology shows the site's decline came mainly from environmental or demographic causes rather than conquest.
questions: How much of the Isokelekel tradition reflects an actual conquest, and how much is later legend explaining Saudeleur rule's end?
How was the labor to move and stack the basalt columns organized, given Pohnpei's small population?

place/nara.title: Nara
place/nara.summary: Nara is a city in Japan's Kansai region that was the capital, then called Heijō-kyō, from 710 to 784 CE, a period in which the Japanese court adopted Chinese models of city planning, writing and state Buddhism.
facts: Heijō-kyō was established as the capital in 710 under Empress Genmei, on a grid plan modeled on the Tang capital Chang'an.
Court scholars compiled the chronicles Kojiki (712) and Nihon Shoki (720) at Nara, written with Chinese characters.
A smallpox epidemic in 735 to 737 is estimated by some historians to have killed a quarter to a third of Japan's population, though the figure is uncertain.
In 743 Emperor Shōmu ordered a giant bronze Buddha, which was dedicated at Tōdai-ji in 752; the statue is about 15 meters tall.
The Shōsōin storehouse at Tōdai-ji preserves objects from the 8th-century court, including items that reflect trade along the Silk Roads.
The court moved to Nagaoka in 784 and to Heian-kyō (Kyoto) in 794, a move often attributed in part to the political influence of Buddhist institutions at Nara.
UNESCO inscribed the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara in 1998.
place/nara.context: Nara imitated Chang'an, the capital of the Tang Dynasty, and was succeeded as the capital by Kyoto. It sits in the Medieval Period and the region East Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief, Art and Ritual and Language and Writing.
place/nara.observer: The Observer notes that Nara shows a court importing a whole order at once: a Chinese city plan, Chinese characters, a state-sponsored Buddhism, and chronicles that used memory-outsourcing to fix the ruling house's origin story in writing. The Great Buddha was ordered a few years after a smallpox epidemic that killed a large part of the population, which suggests that a ruler facing mass death turned to a meaning-engine and to public works, though that link is an inference from the sources. The reading would weaken if the Buddha project proves to have been mainly a response to court rivalries.
questions: How many people died in the epidemic of 735 to 737, and how did the losses affect the court's plans?
Why did the court leave Nara in 784?

place/nazca-lines.title: Nazca Lines
place/nazca-lines.summary: The Nazca Lines are a group of geoglyphs in the desert of southern Peru, made between about 400 BCE and 500 CE by the Paracas and Nazca cultures, showing animal, plant and geometric shapes and hundreds of straight lines visible mainly from the air.
facts: The lines lie in the Nazca Desert between the towns of Nazca and Palpa, about 400 kilometers south of Lima, and cover about 50 square kilometers.
They were made by removing a top layer of reddish, iron-oxide-coated pebbles to expose lighter ground beneath; the lines and figures cut roughly 10 to 15 centimeters deep.
The combined lines run more than 1,300 kilometers, and the largest figures, such as a 134-meter condor and a 93-meter hummingbird, reach lengths of tens to a few hundred meters.

Peruvian archaeologist Toribio Mejía Xesspe noted the lines on foot in 1927; American historian Paul Kosok observed them from the air in 1940 to 1941 and proposed astronomical alignments, a theory developed further by Maria Reiche; researchers Gerald Hawkins and Anthony Aveni concluded in 1990 that the evidence did not support a systematic astronomical purpose.
Other proposed purposes include ritual paths connected to water and fertility, walked in ceremony, and markers tied to underground water sources; no single explanation is agreed on.
UNESCO inscribed the Lines and Geoglyphs of Nazca and Pampas de Jumana in 1994.

The site has been damaged by squatters, a limestone quarry, a 2014 Greenpeace protest that left marks near one geoglyph, and a 2018 truck crossing, and erosion and off-road vehicles remain ongoing threats.
place/nazca-lines.context: The Nazca Lines were made well before the rise of Cusco and the Inca state farther south in the Andes. They sit in the Iron Age and the region Andes, and belong to the theme threads of Religion and Belief and Science.
place/nazca-lines.observer: The Observer notes that a mark made to be read from the ground and a mark made to be read from the air are different kinds of pattern-taming, and the debate over the Lines is partly a debate over which kind their makers intended. Reiche's proposal that they served as an astronomical instrument was a claim about precision that later analysis did not confirm, which the Observer treats as an example of how a compelling reading can outrun its evidence. Because no written record from the makers survives, every purpose offered here is inference from the marks themselves. The reading would weaken if excavation along the lines turns up consistent ritual deposits that point to one purpose over the others.
questions: Were the lines walked as ritual paths, viewed as an observatory, or used for another purpose entirely?
How did the people who made the Lines organize the labor needed to plan and clear such long, straight paths?

place/newgrange.title: Newgrange
place/newgrange.summary: Newgrange is a large passage tomb in the Boyne Valley of County Meath, Ireland, built about 3200 to 3100 BCE by Neolithic farmers and aligned so that the winter solstice sunrise lights its inner chamber.
facts: Newgrange is a mound about 12 meters high and about 85 meters across at its widest, with a passage about 19 meters long leading to a cross-shaped chamber, and radiocarbon dates place its construction at about 3200 to 3100 BCE, older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.
A "roof box" above the entrance admits sunlight along the passage for about 17 minutes around sunrise at the winter solstice.
Kerbstones around the base carry carved designs, including spirals, and cremated remains of a small number of people were found in the chamber.
The white quartz wall at the front was reconstructed in the 1970s, and whether it originally looked like that is debated.
Newgrange was used again in later periods, and Roman coins and other offerings have been found there; later Irish tradition associated the Boyne complex with legendary figures.
Newgrange lies with the nearby passage tombs at Knowth and Dowth, and UNESCO inscribed the Brú na Bóinne complex in 1993.
place/newgrange.context: Newgrange belongs to the farming societies that followed The Agricultural Revolution in Europe, and it stands in the same broad tradition of monuments as Stonehenge; it predates the Giza Necropolis. It sits in the Neolithic and the region Europe, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief, Art and Ritual and Science.
place/newgrange.observer: The Observer notes that Newgrange has a chamber built so that sunrise light at the winter solstice enters for a short time, which suggests careful, sustained observation of the sky by a farming society that had no mark-code to record what the alignment meant. The meaning is inferred: a calendar, a grief-rite for the dead, or both, and the evidence supports the alignment more strongly than any one explanation of its purpose. The reading would weaken if the roof box is shown to be a later addition and not part of the original design.
questions: What did the winter solstice alignment mean to the builders?
How many people built Newgrange, and how long did it take?

place/nile-river.title: Nile River
place/nile-river.summary: The Nile River is a river of northeastern Africa, commonly cited as about 6,650 kilometers long though estimates vary by measurement method, flowing north to the Mediterranean, whose annual flood supported farming and the states of Egypt and Nubia from about the 6th millennium BCE.
facts: The Nile flows north from the highlands of east and central Africa to the Mediterranean; its two main branches, the White Nile from the Lake Victoria region and the Blue Nile from Lake Tana in Ethiopia, meet at Khartoum, and the Ethiopian highlands supply most of the seasonal flood.
Farming communities are documented in the Nile Valley and the Fayum from about the 6th millennium BCE, and the summer flood deposited silt that kept the valley fertile.
Egyptian officials measured the flood on nilometers, and in later periods taxation was tied to its height.
The states of Egypt, after the Unification of Egypt, and of Kush, upstream in Nubia, grew along the river.
The Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970, ended the annual flood in Egypt and created Lake Nasser; about 100,000 Nubians were relocated, and monuments such as Abu Simbel were moved.

Eleven countries share the Nile basin. A 1959 agreement between Egypt and Sudan allocated most of the river's measured flow to those two states, and Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile, begun in 2011 and filled in stages from 2020, is a subject of dispute over water with Egypt and Sudan.
place/nile-river.context: The Nile River is the axis of the Ancient Egyptians and the state formed in the Unification of Egypt, and it linked Egypt with the upstream Kingdom of Kush. It sits in the Neolithic (its earliest farming communities) and the region Nile Valley, and belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life, Trade and Economy and Technology.
place/nile-river.observer: The Observer notes that the Nile turned a predictable flood into a state: a river whose height could be measured, forecast and taxed rewarded record-keeping, an early case of pattern-taming tied to administration. The river's modern history shows that claim-lines drawn across water are harder to keep than lines on land, since a 1959 allocation between two states now faces the claims of upstream countries. The reading would weaken if the flood proves to have been too variable to forecast well enough to shape administration.
questions: How much did variation in the Nile flood affect Egyptian politics and famine?
How will the water of the Nile be shared among the basin countries?

place/paris.title: Paris
place/paris.summary: Paris is the capital of France, on the Seine River, which grew from a settlement of the Gaulish Parisii on the Île de la Cité in about the 3rd century BCE into a Roman town, a medieval capital, a center of revolutions and one of Europe's largest cities.
facts: Paris grew from a settlement of the Parisii on the banks of the Seine between about 250 and 225 BCE, though the exact location of their oppidum, whether the Île de la Cité or Nanterre, is disputed; Rome took the area in 52 BCE and built the town of Lutetia.

Clovis made Paris his capital in about 508, and the Capetian kings made it the center of the French kingdom from 987; Notre-Dame was begun in 1163, and the University of Paris had developed by about 1200.
Paris had perhaps 200,000 inhabitants around 1300, among the largest cities in Europe, and lost a large share of its people to the Black Death in 1348.
The Bastille fell on 14 July 1789 during the French Revolution, and thousands of people were executed in Paris in the Reign of Terror of 1793 to 1794.
Baron Haussmann rebuilt central Paris in the 1850s and 1860s with wide boulevards, sewers and parks.

The suppression of the Paris Commune in 1871 killed many thousands of people in a week of fighting and executions; estimates are contested, ranging from about 7,000 killed in combat or summary execution to a commonly cited 10,000 to 15,000, with a single unconfirmed 1876 estimate as high as 20,000.
Germany occupied Paris from June 1940 to August 1944; in July 1942 French police arrested about 13,000 Jews in the Vel' d'Hiv roundup, most of whom were later deported to Auschwitz.
UNESCO inscribed Paris, Banks of the Seine, in 1991.
place/paris.context: Paris was the stage of the French Revolution and a center of the Enlightenment; it was founded on ground later ruled by the Romans, and under German occupation in World War II it was the scene of roundups that fed the Holocaust. It sits in Classical Antiquity and the region Europe, and belongs to the theme threads of Science, Art and Ritual and War and Conflict.
place/paris.observer: The Observer notes that Paris has repeatedly been remade as a display of the state's story-glue and as a stage for its overthrow: a cathedral for the medieval monarchy, revolutionary crowds, and 19th-century boulevards planned for order and circulation. The same city organized the roundup of its Jewish residents in 1942 and now commemorates it, and the Observer records the deaths of the Terror, the Commune and the deportations as suffering under different regimes. The reading would weaken if the city's monuments prove to have been shaped more by local building needs than by successive regimes' claims.
questions: How large was Paris at its medieval peak, and how did the Black Death change it?
How have the Commune and the 1942 roundup been remembered in French public life?

place/pasargadae.title: Pasargadae
place/pasargadae.summary: Pasargadae was the first capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great in about 550 BCE on the plateau of Fars in present-day Iran, and the site of his tomb.
facts: Pasargadae lies in Fars province, southwestern Iran, about 90 kilometers northeast of Shiraz and about 40 kilometers from Persepolis.
Cyrus the Great founded Pasargadae after defeating the Median king Astyages, in about 550 BCE, and it served as a royal seat until Darius I and his successors developed Persepolis and Susa.
Pasargadae has an audience hall, residential palaces, a gate with a relief of a winged figure, and a formal garden with water channels that is regarded as an early example of the Persian garden.

Stonemasons from other parts of the empire, including Lydia and Ionia in western Anatolia, contributed to its masonry, and its architecture combines Persian, Elamite, Mesopotamian and Anatolian elements.
The Tomb of Cyrus, a stepped base topped by a gabled stone chamber, stands at the site; Greek writers report that Alexander visited it and ordered its restoration after it had been robbed.
Inscriptions naming Cyrus appear at Pasargadae, though some scholars argue that they were added under Darius I.
UNESCO inscribed Pasargadae in 2004.
place/pasargadae.context: Pasargadae was the first capital of the Achaemenid Persians and was later overshadowed by Persepolis. Cyrus, its founder, took Babylon in 539 BCE, and Alexander visited the site during Alexander's Conquests. Pasargadae sits in the Iron Age and the region Iranian Plateau, and belongs to the theme threads of Art and Ritual, War and Conflict and Religion and Belief.
place/pasargadae.observer: The Observer notes that Pasargadae shows an empire assembling its style from its subjects: masons from Lydia, motifs from Mesopotamia and Elam, and a garden layout later copied across Persian courts, an exchange-web of craftsmen and ideas made visible in stone. A founder's tomb that a later conqueror chose to visit and restore suggests that story-glue about kingship could pass across dynasties and even across enemies. The reading would weaken if the building phases prove to belong mostly to Darius I, since the site would then tell more about a later king's claim on Cyrus's legacy.

What were the roles of Pasargadae and Persepolis in court ritual?

place/persepolis.title: Persepolis
place/persepolis.summary: Persepolis was a ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire in southwestern Iran, begun around 518 BCE under Darius I and burned by Alexander the Great's army in 330 BCE.
facts: Construction began under Darius I around 518 BCE and continued under his successors.
The Apadana reliefs show delegations from across the empire bringing gifts.
Alexander's army burned the palace in 330 BCE; ancient sources give conflicting motives, including revenge and drunken impulse.
Thousands of Elamite tablets, the Persepolis Fortification Tablets, record rations and administration.
It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1979.
place/persepolis.context: Persepolis embodies the imperial ideology of the Achaemenid Persians founded by Cyrus the Great, and its destruction was part of Alexander's Conquests. Persepolis sits in the Iron Age and the region Iranian Plateau, and belongs to the theme thread of Art and Ritual and War and Conflict.
place/persepolis.observer: The Observer notes that the reliefs show subject peoples arriving with tribute in orderly procession, an image of empire as harmonious exchange. Every empire tells its own story in stone, and the stone lasts longer than the story's rivals.
questions: Was the burning of Persepolis deliberate policy or an accident?

place/petra.title: Petra
place/petra.summary: Petra is a rock-cut city in the mountains of southern Jordan that served as the capital of the Nabataean kingdom from about the 2nd century BCE until Rome annexed the kingdom in 106 CE.
facts: Petra lies in a basin among sandstone mountains, entered through a gorge about 1.2 kilometers long known as the Siq.
Greek writers describe an expedition against the Nabataeans in 312 BCE and their rock refuge, which is sometimes identified with Petra, though the identification is doubtful.

Petra's carved facades, including al-Khazneh ("the Treasury"), date mostly from about the 1st century BCE to the 1st century CE. Most facades are thought to be tombs, though the use of some, including the Treasury, is debated.

Petra was supplied by dams, channels, ceramic pipes and cisterns in a desert climate, and its wealth is generally attributed to the caravan trade in incense and other goods. Estimates of its peak population are uncertain, with about 20,000 commonly cited and some figures as high as 30,000.

After Roman annexation in 106 CE, Petra became part of the province of Arabia. An earthquake in 363 CE destroyed many buildings and the city declined afterward; the Swiss traveler Johann Ludwig Burckhardt brought it to European attention in 1812.
UNESCO inscribed Petra in 1985.
place/petra.context: Petra was the capital of the Nabataeans and a node in the Incense Trade before its annexation by the Romans; its sister site is Hegra in Saudi Arabia. The site lies in Jordan, at the northern edge of the region Arabian Peninsula. Petra sits in Classical Antiquity and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and Art and Ritual.
place/petra.observer: The Observer notes that Petra's most visible investment, the carved facades, is largely funerary, so a trading people's wealth became permanent chiefly as grief-rites and status-signals for the dead, while the caravans left little trace. A city that lived on stored water and control of a passage, not on farmland, shows how control of a route can stand in for control of land. The reading depends on the tomb attribution, which is well supported for many facades but debated for others such as the Treasury.
questions: What were the carved buildings of Petra used for, and how many were tombs, banquet halls or temples?
What did Petra depend on after the caravan routes shifted?

place/pompeii.title: Pompeii
place/pompeii.summary: Pompeii was a Roman town on the Bay of Naples in Italy, founded in about the 7th century BCE, that was buried under volcanic ash and pumice when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE.
facts: Pompeii was founded in about the 7th century BCE by the Oscans, came under Greek and Etruscan influence, and became a Roman colony in 80 BCE.
An earthquake in 62 or 63 CE damaged the town, and repairs were still under way when Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE.
Pompeii's population is estimated at about 11,000, with estimates ranging from about 10,000 to 20,000.

The eruption buried Pompeii under pumice and ash, and pyroclastic surges killed people who had stayed; about 1,100 bodies have been found in the excavated town, and many inhabitants are thought to have fled.
The traditional date of the eruption is 24 August, but a charcoal inscription found in 2018 suggests a later date, possibly in October.

Excavations began in 1748, and in 1863 Giuseppe Fiorelli began pouring plaster into voids left by decayed bodies to produce casts of victims; graffiti, shop signs and election notices survive on the walls.
UNESCO inscribed the archaeological areas of Pompeii, Herculaneum and Torre Annunziata in 1997.
place/pompeii.context: Pompeii was a town of the Romans and part of the wider world governed from Rome. It sits in the Iron Age (its Oscan foundation) and the region Mediterranean Basin, and belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life, Trade and Economy and Art and Ritual.
place/pompeii.observer: The Observer notes that Pompeii is a case where a natural catastrophe left an unusually complete record of ordinary life, shop signs, graffiti, bakeries and casts, an unintended act of memory-outsourcing that no one planned. The Observer records the deaths of the people found there as suffering, and notes that the casts of victims raise the question of how such remains should be shown. The record is biased toward one town on one day and toward what was left behind, and the reading would weaken if new counts show that the number of people who died was much smaller or larger than the current figures suggest.

place/port-royal.title: Port Royal
place/port-royal.summary: Port Royal was an English port town at the tip of the Palisadoes spit at the entrance to Kingston Harbour, Jamaica, which grew after 1655 as a base for privateers and traders and lost about two-thirds of its area to an earthquake on 7 June 1692.
facts: England took Jamaica from Spain in 1655, and Port Royal was fortified from 1656; English governors issued commissions to privateers, who used the port as a base to attack Spanish ships and towns.
Henry Morgan, a privateer who later became lieutenant governor of Jamaica, led raids from the colony, including the sack of Panama in 1671.
Port Royal was a trading port for the island's goods and a landing and sale point for enslaved Africans; it had about 6,500 residents in 1692.

On 7 June 1692 an earthquake, and the liquefaction of the sandy ground beneath the town, sank about two-thirds of Port Royal into the harbor. About 2,000 people are estimated to have died in the quake and its immediate aftermath, and several thousand more died of injury and disease in the following weeks.
Some contemporary accounts read the earthquake as divine judgment.
Survivors founded Kingston across the harbor, a fire in 1703 destroyed much of what remained of Port Royal, and the Royal Navy used the town as a base into the early 20th century.
Underwater archaeology from the 1950s, and again from the 1980s, has recovered buildings and household objects from the submerged area.
place/port-royal.context: Port Royal grew as the English Caribbean took shape after the Spanish colony at Santo Domingo had already set the pattern of European settlement, and its trade touched the Atlantic Slave Trade and the Sugar Plantation Complex. It sits in the Early Modern Period and the region Caribbean and Atlantic World, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, War and Conflict and Earth Systems and Life.
place/port-royal.observer: The Observer notes a port whose wealth came from state-licensed raiding and from trade that included the sale of enslaved people, and whose sudden loss some contemporaries explained through their own meaning-engine as divine judgment. The sinking also froze a working town's daily life in place, an unusual case in which a disaster acts as memory-outsourcing for people who left few documents. The popular image of Port Royal as uniquely lawless is a later story-glue, and how far the record supports it is debated. A historian could challenge the first sentence by showing that privateering brought the town less wealth than ordinary trade did.
questions: How much of Port Royal's wealth came from privateering, from ordinary trade and from the sale of enslaved people?
How much of the submerged town remains to be recorded?

place/poverty-point.title: Poverty Point
place/poverty-point.summary: Poverty Point is a large earthwork complex in Louisiana built by hunter-gatherer-fishers between about 1700 and 1100 BCE, with concentric ridges and huge mounds.
facts: The site has six concentric earthen ridges and several mounds, the largest about 22 meters high.
It was built by a society without agriculture, according to current evidence.
Stone and other materials were brought from across the Mississippi valley, some from hundreds of kilometers away.
It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2014.
The site was abandoned around 1100 BCE.

place/rapa-nui.title: Rapa Nui
place/rapa-nui.summary: Rapa Nui (Easter Island) is a remote Pacific island settled by Polynesians around 1200 CE, famous for nearly a thousand monumental stone statues called moai.
facts: The island lies in the southeastern Pacific, thousands of kilometers from the nearest large land.
Estimates for the arrival of the Polynesian settlers range from as early as about 300 CE, based on contested early radiocarbon dates, to about 1200 CE, the date favored by many recent studies.

About 400 moai (397 in one count) lie in the quarry of Rano Raraku in various stages of completion, and about 95 percent of the island's monolithic statues were carved from its volcanic tuff. Published counts of the total number of moai differ.

The popular story of self-inflicted ecological collapse is contested. Researchers point to introduced rats, which may have been the main cause of deforestation, and to disease and slave raids. In December 1862 Peruvian slavers captured about 1,000 islanders, and reports put the total taken in 1862 to 1864 at more than 1,400. Most of the captives died in Peru, and a smallpox epidemic that followed the return of a few survivors in 1863 reportedly killed about a thousand more. These figures come from popular summaries and vary between accounts.
Rapa Nui National Park was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1995.
place/rapa-nui.context: Rapa Nui was the far eastern edge of the Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific and of the Polynesians' voyaging world. Rapa Nui sits in the Medieval Period and the region Oceania, and belongs to the theme thread of Art and Ritual and Earth Systems and Life.
place/rapa-nui.observer: The Observer notes that the island is often told as a parable of self-destruction, but the record suggests that outside pressures did much of the damage. Stories that fit a moral are chosen more readily than stories that fit the evidence.
questions: How large was the population at its peak, and what caused its decline?

place/robben-island.title: Robben Island
place/robben-island.summary: Robben Island is a small island in Table Bay, about 7 kilometers off Cape Town, South Africa, used from the 17th century to 1996 as a place of banishment, a leprosy colony and a prison, and best known for the political prisoners held there under apartheid, including Nelson Mandela.
facts: Robben Island lies in Table Bay about 7 kilometers from Cape Town and covers about 5 square kilometers; its name comes from the Dutch word for seals.
The Dutch East India Company began using Robben Island as a place of banishment in the 1650s; among those sent there was the Khoikhoi interpreter Autshumato, in 1658.
A leprosy colony operated on the island from 1845, with no firmly documented closure date, and it served as a military base in the Second World War.
From 1961 Robben Island held political prisoners under apartheid, including Nelson Mandela (imprisoned on the island for 18 of his 27 years, from 1964), Robert Sobukwe, Walter Sisulu and Govan Mbeki.
Prisoners worked in a limestone quarry, and the glare damaged Mandela's eyes; prisoners organized study and debate among themselves, and the prison was nicknamed a "university".
The maximum-security political prison closed in 1991; a separate medium-security prison on the island for criminal prisoners closed in 1996.
UNESCO inscribed Robben Island in 1999, and former prisoners lead tours of the island today.
place/robben-island.context: Robben Island was first used as a place of banishment by the Dutch East India Company, and its years as an apartheid prison belong to the wider struggle over minority rule in the period of Decolonization. It sits in the Early Modern Period and the region Sub-Saharan Africa, and belongs to the theme threads of War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
place/robben-island.observer: The Observer notes that Robben Island shows water used as a wall: for more than three centuries authorities sent people they wanted removed from society, exiles, patients and dissidents, to a place where isolation was cheap to enforce. The same isolation concentrated a generation of leaders who studied and argued together, so a prison also worked as a school and an exchange-web of ideas, an outcome its designers did not intend, and the Observer records the years of imprisonment and forced labor as suffering. The reading would weaken if accounts of prisoners' study and organization describe only a small, unrepresentative part of the prison population.
questions: How did prisoners on Robben Island organize themselves, and how far did their organization reach beyond the island?
How should the island present its earlier uses, such as the leprosy colony and the exile of Khoikhoi leaders?

place/rock-hewn-churches-of-lalibela.title: Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela
place/rock-hewn-churches-of-lalibela.summary: The Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela are eleven churches carved down into volcanic rock in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, traditionally attributed to King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty in the early 13th century and still in use for worship.
facts: Lalibela lies at about 2,500 meters in the Amhara Region of Ethiopia and has eleven monolithic churches, in two main groups and one separate cross-shaped church, Bete Giyorgis.
The churches are traditionally attributed to King Lalibela, who reigned around the late 12th and early 13th centuries; some scholars propose that some churches are older.

Builders first cut trenches into the rock and then carved the exterior and interior of each church from the block left standing, joining the churches by trenches and tunnels and cutting drainage channels.

Lalibela is presented in tradition as a "New Jerusalem", with features named after places in the Holy Land, such as a stream called the Jordan; the link with the loss of Jerusalem to Saladin in 1187 is traditional and is not documented in contemporary sources.
The churches remain in active use, and large numbers of pilgrims come at major festivals.
UNESCO inscribed the Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela in 1978.
place/rock-hewn-churches-of-lalibela.context: The Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela were built under the Zagwe Dynasty in a region shaped earlier by the Kingdom of Aksum and its town Aksum, and the "New Jerusalem" tradition relates them to the time of the Crusades. They sit in the Medieval Period and the region Sub-Saharan Africa, and belong to the theme threads of Religion and Belief, Art and Ritual and Technology.
place/rock-hewn-churches-of-lalibela.observer: The Observer notes that Lalibela reverses the usual order of building: workers removed rock and did not add it, cutting free-standing churches down into the ground, a labor-heavy technique that also makes the buildings hard to destroy. The "New Jerusalem" tradition shows a place made to stand in for a distant sacred site when access to the original was in doubt, a meaning-engine adjusting to political change. Because the link to 1187 is not documented in contemporary sources, the reading would weaken if the churches prove to have been planned around a different rationale.
questions: Which of the churches were built in the reign of Lalibela, and which are earlier or later?
How many workers were involved, and how long did the carving take?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: King Gebre Meskel Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty ruled c. 1181-1221, the reign to which the churches are traditionally attributed, though scholars debate the construction dates [Wikipedia on Lalibela; Wikipedia on Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela]

2026-09-27: The site comprises eleven monolithic churches: five north of the river Jordan, five south of it, and one independently located cruciform church, Bete Giyorgis (Church of Saint George) [Wikipedia on Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela]

2026-09-27: The layout and names of the major buildings at Lalibela are widely accepted as a symbolic representation of Jerusalem, and the article suggests a possible link to Saladin's capture of Jerusalem in 1187 [Wikipedia on Lalibela]

facts: Rome had roughly a million inhabitants in the first two centuries CE, by many estimates.
The Colosseum was completed in 80 CE.
The city was sacked in 410 and 455 CE.
It later became the seat of the papacy.

place/samarkand.title: Samarkand
place/samarkand.summary: Samarkand is a city in present-day Uzbekistan, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities of Central Asia and a leading crossroads of the Silk Roads.
facts: The ancient city (Afrasiab) is thought to date from the 7th century BCE or earlier.
It was known to the Greeks as Maracanda and was taken by Alexander the Great in 329 BCE.
It was a major Sogdian city, was sacked by Genghis Khan in 1220, and became Timur's capital in the 1370s.
UNESCO inscribed 'Samarkand - Crossroad of Cultures' in 2001.

place/santo-domingo.title: Santo Domingo
place/santo-domingo.summary: Santo Domingo is the capital of the Dominican Republic, on the south coast of Hispaniola, founded by Spain in 1496 and commonly described as the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the Americas.
facts: Santo Domingo was founded in 1496 by Bartholomew Columbus on the east bank of the Ozama River, and governor Nicolás de Ovando moved it to the west bank in 1502 after storm damage.

Santo Domingo became the seat of Spanish administration in the Caribbean, with the first Real Audiencia in the Americas (created by royal decree in 1511, with its start of operation dated differently by sources), a cathedral begun in the 1510s and completed in 1540, and a university founded in 1538.
Expeditions to Puerto Rico, Cuba and the mainland were organized from Hispaniola under this colonial administration.

The Taíno population of Hispaniola fell sharply under forced labor, violence and disease, including a smallpox epidemic beginning in 1518. Estimates of the pre-contact population range from tens of thousands to over a million, and a Spanish count in 1514 recorded about 26,000 Taíno on the island.

Enslaved Africans were brought to Hispaniola from the early 1500s; in December 1521 enslaved Africans rebelled on a sugar estate near the city, an uprising commonly described as the first of its kind in the Americas.
UNESCO inscribed the Colonial City of Santo Domingo in 1990.
place/santo-domingo.context: Santo Domingo was the base for the first phase of the Columbian Exchange in the Caribbean, which brought devastation to the Taino and drew the island into the Atlantic Slave Trade and the Sugar Plantation Complex. Its administrators and settlers later took part in the Spanish Conquest of the Aztec Empire and other mainland ventures. The city stands on Hispaniola, in the Early Modern Period and the region Caribbean and Atlantic World, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, War and Conflict and Religion and Belief.
place/santo-domingo.observer: The Observer notes that within about four decades Spain had placed a high court, a cathedral and a university on a shore where none had stood, extending a claim-line through stone institutions while the people already on the island were drawn into a forced-labor system. The city marks a point where two exchange-webs, one from Europe and one from the Americas, began moving people, crops and pathogens in both directions. The rebellion of 1521 shows that those held in the system resisted it from early on. Because the population figures rest on Spanish colonial counts, the size of the Taíno loss is uncertain even though its direction is not.
questions: How large was the pre-contact population of Hispaniola, and how much of its decline came from disease compared with forced labor and violence?
How did Santo Domingo's role change as Spain's attention shifted to the mainland?

place/sarai.title: Sarai
place/sarai.summary: Sarai was the capital of the Golden Horde, the western part of the Mongol Empire, on the lower Volga River in present-day southern Russia, founded around 1250 by Batu Khan and sacked by Timur in 1395.
facts: Batu Khan, a grandson of Chinggis Khan, founded Sarai (Persian for "palace") on the lower Volga; William of Rubruck's account of 1253 to 1254 is the first historical reference, so "about 1250" is an approximation. Scholars now doubt that a separate city called Sarai of Berke ever existed; the standard pairing is Old Sarai (Batu's, exact location undetermined) and New Sarai, founded or inaugurated by Öz Beg Khan around 1334 to 1335 and now generally identified with the Selitrennoye site in Astrakhan Oblast.
Rus' princes traveled to Sarai to pay tribute and receive a yarlyk (charter) confirming their rule, and an Orthodox bishopric of Sarai was established in 1261.
Öz Beg Khan (reigned 1313 to 1341) adopted Islam as the Horde's state religion.
The traveler Ibn Battuta visited in the 1330s and described a large city with markets and people of many nations.
Plague reached the Black Sea port of Caffa in 1346 during a siege by Golden Horde forces and spread from there through Mediterranean ports; the Horde's role in its spread is debated.

Timur sacked and burned Sarai in the winter of 1395 to 1396 in his war with Khan Tokhtamysh; the city partially recovered by 1402 and was minting coins again by the 1420s, though it never regained its former status as capital.
place/sarai.context: Sarai was the capital of the Golden Horde, a successor state of the Mongol Empire created by the Mongol Conquests, and it was sacked by forces of Timur, founder of the Timurid Empire. It lay on trade routes linked to the spread of the Black Death. Sarai sits in the Medieval Period and the region Central Asian Steppe, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, War and Conflict and Religion and Belief.
place/sarai.observer: The Observer notes that Sarai was a capital whose main function was to collect and pass on tribute, and where rulers of distant cities came to be confirmed in office by a document that could be withdrawn, a claim-line maintained by paperwork as much as by garrisons. A steppe empire that moved between camps also built permanent cities with mosques and workshops, and Sarai housed several religions under one authority. The period is remembered differently in Russian, Tatar and Central Asian national histories, so the same evidence supports several stories. Historians who stress the Horde's role as a trading partner and not an overlord would challenge the first sentence.
questions: How large was Sarai, and how did its population change over time?
Which of the two Sarais served as the capital at different times?

2026-09-27: Öz Beg Khan founded or formally inaugurated New Sarai around 1334-1335, roughly 78 miles north of Old Sarai, and the present general consensus identifies the Selitrennoye gorodishche as New Sarai while there is no consensus on where Old Sarai stood [Wikipedia on Sarai (city)]

place/stonehenge.title: Stonehenge
place/stonehenge.summary: Stonehenge is a monument of standing stones on Salisbury Plain in southern England, begun as a circular earthwork around 3000 BCE and rebuilt in stone over the next several centuries.
facts: The first phase was a circular ditch and bank, around 3000 BCE.
The large sarsen stones, of which the biggest weigh around 25 tons, were sourced from around 25 kilometers away, according to a 2020 study identifying West Woods as the source.
The smaller bluestones were brought from the Preseli Hills in Wales, more than 200 kilometers away.
A 2024 study reported that the Altar Stone came from northern Scotland, roughly 750 kilometers away.
The site was used for burials, with cremated remains from early in its history, and its axis aligns with the solstice sunrise and sunset.
place/stonehenge.context: Stonehenge shows that farming communities in Britain could organize large collective labor and long-distance transport before metal tools. It stands alongside monuments such as Giza Necropolis as an example of monumental building in the Neolithic and Bronze Age. Stonehenge sits in the Neolithic and the region Europe, and belongs to the theme thread of Religion and Belief and Art and Ritual.
place/stonehenge.observer: The Observer notes that people moved multi-ton stones over long distances and aligned them to the sun, without a written record of why. Monuments outlast the meanings that produced them, and the meaning is then rebuilt by each generation of visitors.
questions: What was the site used for, and by whom?
How were the largest stones moved?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Sarsens from West Woods about 25 km away (2020); Altar Stone from northeast Scotland, at least 750 km (2024) [Nash et al. 2020 Origins of the Sarsen Megaliths at Stonehenge; Clarke et al. 2024 Scottish Provenance of the Altar Stone]

place/taj-mahal.title: Taj Mahal
place/taj-mahal.summary: The Taj Mahal is a white marble mausoleum in Agra, built from about 1632 to 1653 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631.
facts: Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631 while giving birth.
Construction began in 1632, with the main tomb largely finished by about 1643 and the complex by 1653.
Commonly cited estimates give around 20,000 workers.
Ustad Ahmad Lahori is often named as its chief architect, though attribution is debated.
It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1983.
place/taj-mahal.context: The Taj Mahal is the best known monument of the Mughal Empire and blends Persian, Islamic, and Indian building traditions. Taj Mahal sits in the Early Modern Period and the region South Asia, and belongs to the theme thread of Art and Ritual and Kinship and Society.
place/taj-mahal.observer: The Observer notes that an emperor with the resources of a large state used them to build a tomb for one person. The world's most visited grief-rite is also one of its greatest displays of state power, and the two cannot be separated.
questions: Who designed the Taj Mahal?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Mumtaz Mahal died 1631; construction 1632-1653; over 20,000 workers; Ahmad Lahori probable architect; UNESCO 1983 [Taj Mahal Official Site and History Sources]

place/tenochtitlan.title: Tenochtitlan
place/tenochtitlan.summary: Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztec Empire, founded on an island in Lake Texcoco in 1325 and destroyed after a siege in 1521.
facts: Population estimates for 1519 range from about 100,000 to 400,000, with 200,000 often cited, making it one of the largest cities in the world.
Causeways and canals connected it to the mainland; chinampas provided food.
The Templo Mayor was its main temple.
Mexico City was built over its ruins.
place/tenochtitlan.context: Tenochtitlan was the center of the Aztec Empire. Its fall is part of the Columbian Exchange.
place/tenochtitlan.observer: The Observer notes that the Spanish visitors described the city with awe. The destruction of such a city in a single siege is a sharp example of how disease and alliances can decide events.
questions: What was the population before the epidemic?

place/teotihuacan.title: Teotihuacan
place/teotihuacan.summary: Teotihuacan was a huge planned city in the Valley of Mexico that flourished from about 100 BCE to 550 CE, home to the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon.
facts: At its peak, around 450 to 500 CE, it may have had 125,000 to 200,000 inhabitants.
The city was laid out on a grid along the 'Avenue of the Dead'.
It had wide trade and political links, including with Maya cities.
The Aztecs later gave it its name, meaning roughly 'place where the gods were created'.
place/teotihuacan.context: Teotihuacan influenced the Maya and other peoples of Mesoamerica.
place/teotihuacan.observer: The Observer notes that its builders left no deciphered writing, and that later peoples treated the ruins as sacred. Even ruins are read through a later culture's meaning-engine.
questions: Who ruled Teotihuacan, and why did it collapse?

place/tikal.title: Tikal
place/tikal.summary: Tikal is a large Maya city in the rainforest of northern Guatemala, with traces of farming from about 1000 BCE, a dominant Classic-period kingdom whose rulers left inscriptions from the 3rd to the 9th century CE, and a city almost deserted after about 950.
facts: Tikal, called Yax Mutal in inscriptions and the seat of a kingdom called Mutul, lies in the Petén region of Guatemala; traces of farming date to about 1000 BCE, and monumental building began about 400 to 300 BCE.

Inscriptions record that in January 378 a warlord named Siyaj K'ak' arrived from the west and Tikal's king died the same day; a new king linked to Teotihuacan was then installed, and scholars debate whether the event was a conquest or an alliance.
In 562 Tikal was defeated by Calakmul and Caracol and its king was apparently captured and sacrificed; in 695 Jasaw Chan K'awiil I defeated Calakmul, and Tikal revived.
Estimates of Tikal's peak population range from about 10,000 to 90,000 for the city, with far higher numbers proposed for its surrounding region, and archaeologists debate them.
The last dated monument was set up in 869, and after about 950 Tikal was almost deserted, during the wider Classic Maya collapse.

Modesto Méndez and Ambrosio Tut visited in 1848, Alfred Maudslay documented the site in 1881 to 1882, and the University of Pennsylvania excavated it from 1956 to 1970; Guatemala made it a national park in 1955 and UNESCO inscribed it in 1979.
place/tikal.context: Tikal was one of the largest kingdoms of the Maya and had ties to Teotihuacan in central Mexico; its emptying is part of the Classic Maya Collapse. Tikal sits in the Iron Age by its earliest settlement, with its peak in the Medieval Period, in the region Mesoamerica, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief, War and Conflict and Language and Writing.
place/tikal.observer: The Observer notes that Tikal's kings set their wars, accessions and rites in stone in a mark-code, so the city's political history is read largely through the claims of its rulers, which favor legitimacy. Temples raised over royal tombs tied the ruler's body to the standing of the city, a status-signal built to be seen across the forest, and the emptying of the city shows that a monument-building center can be left within a few generations. The reading would weaken if epigraphic and archaeological work shows that non-royal households, not kings, drove most decisions about settlement and abandonment.
questions: How large was Tikal's population at its peak, and how was it fed and supplied with water?
Was the event of 378 a conquest by Teotihuacan or an alliance between elites?

place/timbuktu.title: Timbuktu
place/timbuktu.summary: Timbuktu is a city in Mali on the southern edge of the Sahara that became a hub of the trans-Saharan trade and of Islamic scholarship.
facts: It was founded around 1100 CE as a seasonal camp.
Salt from the Sahara and gold from the south were traded there.
The Sankore mosque and madrasa were centers of learning.
It holds hundreds of thousands of historical manuscripts and was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988.
place/timbuktu.context: See Mali Empire and Mansa Musa.
place/timbuktu.observer: The Observer notes that a city at the edge of a desert became famous as a repository of knowledge. Manuscript libraries in private homes were another form of distributed memory.
questions: What do the surviving manuscripts contain?

place/troy.title: Troy
place/troy.summary: Troy is an archaeological site at Hisarlık in northwestern Turkey, occupied from about 3000 BCE into the Byzantine era in nine main layers, and identified by many scholars as the city of Homer's Iliad.
facts: Troy stands at Hisarlık, near the Dardanelles in Çanakkale Province, Turkey; excavators distinguish nine main settlement layers, Troy I to Troy IX, beginning around 3000 BCE.
Heinrich Schliemann began excavations at Troy in 1870, and later excavators included Wilhelm Dörpfeld, Carl Blegen and Manfred Korfmann.

Schliemann's "Treasure of Priam" came from Troy II, about 2500 BCE, far older than any Trojan War; he took it out of the Ottoman Empire, it disappeared from Berlin in 1945 and resurfaced in Moscow in the 1990s.

Troy VI (about 1700 to 1300 BCE) was a large fortified city, and Troy VIIa was destroyed by fire around 1180 BCE and is often proposed as the city of the Trojan War, if the war has a historical basis.
Hittite texts mention a land called Wilusa in western Anatolia, whose name is often linked to Ilios, a Greek name for Troy; the identification is debated.
Whether a Trojan War took place is unknown; the Iliad was composed in Greek around the 8th century BCE, centuries after the events it describes.
Greeks and Romans later built the city of Ilion at the site, and UNESCO inscribed Troy in 1998.
place/troy.context: Troy had the Hittites and the Mycenaean Greeks as neighbors and was remembered by the later Ancient Greeks; Alexander visited it in 334 BCE during Alexander's Conquests. The destruction of Troy VIIa falls close in time to the Bronze Age Collapse. It sits in the Bronze Age and the region Levant and Anatolia, and belongs to the theme threads of War and Conflict, Art and Ritual and Language and Writing.
place/troy.observer: The Observer notes that Troy is a place where a story led to a spade: Schliemann set out to find the city of the Iliad and did find a city, though not necessarily the city of the poem, which shows how a narrative can direct an excavation and then be mistaken for its evidence. The poem's story-glue gave the site a long life as a destination, from Alexander to modern tourists. The reading would weaken if the identification of Wilusa with Troy is refuted, or if Troy VIIa proves unrelated to any historical conflict.
questions: Did a war take place at Troy, and if so, in which layer?
How large was the population of Troy VI?

2026-09-27: Priam's Treasure was found by Schliemann, who proposed Troy II as the city of legend, but later research showed Troy II (built around 2550 BCE, destroyed around 2300 BCE) predated the Mycenaean era by several hundred years [Wikipedia on Troy]

place/uluru.title: Uluru
place/uluru.summary: Uluru is a large sandstone inselberg in central Australia, sacred to the Anangu people, who have been associated with the site for more than 10,000 years and hold traditional custodianship of it today.
facts: Uluru rises 348 meters above the surrounding plain (863 meters above sea level) and lies about 335 kilometers southwest of Alice Springs; it is composed of arkose sandstone whose lack of internal jointing has left it largely free of scree slopes.

Archaeological evidence shows human presence in the area for more than 10,000 years; the date_start of -8000 is a round figure within that range, and older evidence for the peopling of the surrounding region belongs to a different brief.

The Anangu, whose Pitjantjatjara and Yankunytjatjara traditions call the rock's stories Tjukurpa, hold that ancestral beings shaped the landscape, and some tracks and sites at Uluru carry restrictions tied to gender and ceremony.

Surveyor William Gosse named the formation Ayers Rock on 19 July 1873; the government returned ownership to the local Pitjantjatjara people on 26 October 1985, under a 99-year lease-back and joint management arrangement, and dual naming (later reordered to Uluru / Ayers Rock in 2002) followed in 1993.

The Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park board voted in 2017 to end recreational climbing, which had long concerned the Anangu as crossing a sacred track and as a safety risk; the ban took effect on 26 October 2019.
UNESCO inscribed Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park in 1987.
place/uluru.context: Uluru has been significant to the Aboriginal Australians since long after the Peopling of Sahul first brought people to the continent, and its handback in 1985 and the 2019 climbing ban came long after the disruption of the First Fleet and the Colonization of Australia. It sits in the Holocene Epoch and the region Oceania, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief and Earth Systems and Life.
place/uluru.observer: The Observer notes that Uluru carried two names and two systems of meaning at once for over a century, a European name attached by a surveyor and a body of Tjukurpa tradition held by the Anangu, and that the 1985 handback and the 2019 climbing ban both moved authority over the site back toward the tradition that predates the European name. Treating Tjukurpa as tradition rather than as folklore to be judged is a deliberate choice made here, following the same standard applied to other traditions in this record. The reading would weaken if the closure of the climb is shown to have been driven mainly by liability concerns rather than respect for Anangu wishes.
questions: How has joint management under the 1985 agreement changed decisions about the site since then?
How many of the deaths and injuries associated with the former climbing route shaped the 2017 decision, alongside the Anangu's own long-standing requests?

place/upano-valley-settlements.title: Upano Valley Settlements
place/upano-valley-settlements.summary: The Upano Valley settlements are a network of ancient urban centers in the Ecuadorian Amazon, documented by lidar and reported in 2024, occupied from about 500 BCE for many centuries.
facts: The network spans roughly 300 square kilometers (about 115 square miles) and includes some 15 urban centers.
More than 6,000 rectangular earthen platforms, probably house and civic foundations, are linked by roads and drainage canals.
The valley probably held at least 10,000 farmers, and possibly many more, about 2,000 years ago.
The population began to leave between about 300 and 600 CE; the reasons are unknown.
place/upano-valley-settlements.context: The valley is among the earliest known Amazonian urban settlements. See Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths and Casarabe Culture.
place/upano-valley-settlements.observer: The Observer notes that these settlements are roughly contemporary with Rome's rise yet were unknown to science until laser mapping stripped away the forest. Absence from the record can reflect what was not yet looked for.
questions: Who lived in the Upano Valley, and why did they leave?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Built about 500 BCE; about 15 urban centers; more than 6,000 platforms; at least 10,000 farmers; population left about 300-600 CE [Smithsonian on the Upano Valley (Rostain et al. 2024)]

place/ur.title: Ur
place/ur.summary: Ur was a Sumerian city in southern Iraq, occupied from about 3800 BCE and abandoned around 500 BCE, known for its Great Ziggurat, its royal cemetery, and its role as the capital of the Third Dynasty of Ur about 2100 BCE.
facts: Ur lies at Tell el-Muqayyar in Dhi Qar Governorate, southern Iraq, near the Euphrates; it was occupied by the late Ubaid period and grew into a city in the 3rd millennium BCE.

Leonard Woolley excavated Ur from 1922 to 1934 and found a royal cemetery dated to about 2600 to 2500 BCE, with graves holding gold and lapis lazuli jewelry, lyres and, in some, the bodies of many attendants placed with the dead; how the attendants died is debated.
Enheduanna, a daughter of Sargon of Akkad and high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur about 2300 BCE, is the earliest named author known.
Ur-Nammu (reigned about 2112 to 2095 BCE) founded the Third Dynasty of Ur, built the Great Ziggurat for Nanna, and is credited with the earliest surviving law code.
Ur fell to Elamite forces about 2004 BCE and later became a smaller city; it was abandoned around 500 BCE, and proposed causes include a shift in the Euphrates and drier conditions.
The biblical "Ur of the Chaldees", birthplace of Abraham, is often identified with Ur, but the identification is debated.
UNESCO included Ur in the "Ahwar of Southern Iraq" listing in 2016.
place/ur.context: Ur was a city of the Sumerians alongside Uruk, and it belongs to the story of The Urban Revolution and the Invention of Writing in southern Mesopotamia. It sits in the Bronze Age and the region Mesopotamia, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief, Trade and Economy and Language and Writing.
place/ur.observer: The Observer notes that the royal cemetery of Ur preserves an early case of attendants buried with a ruler, a grief-rite and status-signal in one; whether they died willingly, under coercion or in a ritual understood as honor cannot be settled from the bones, and the Observer records the possibility of coerced death as suffering. A city whose temple priestess is the first named author and whose ruler issued an early law code suggests an early state that used mark-code to bind rule to the gods. The reading would weaken if new studies show that the burials differ from those of other early Mesopotamian cities in ways that make Ur unrepresentative.
questions: How did the attendants in the Royal Cemetery die, and did they take part willingly?
Why was Ur abandoned around 500 BCE?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Ur stood at Tell el-Muqayyar in Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq, was settled from the Ubaid period about 3800 BC, was abandoned after 500 BC, and its decline is linked to drought, changing river patterns and silting of the outlet to the Persian Gulf [Wikipedia on Ur]

2026-09-27: Charles Leonard Woolley led the major excavation of Ur from 1922 to 1934 and uncovered about 1,850 burials, including 16 royal tombs dated to around 2600 BC, where CT scans of some surviving skulls show signs of blows to the head, contradicting the older theory of voluntary mass death by poisoning [Wikipedia on Ur]

2026-09-27: Ur-Nammu founded the Third Dynasty of Ur and ruled about 2112 to 2094 BC on the Middle Chronology, and the Code of Ur-Namma is described as the earliest of its genre though it survives only in fragmentary late copies [Wikipedia on Third Dynasty of Ur]

2026-09-27: The Third Dynasty of Ur fell around 2004 BC on the Middle Chronology to a coalition of Elamite troops, while the low chronology dates the dynasty to 2048 to 1940 BC [Wikipedia on Third Dynasty of Ur]

2026-09-27: Enheduanna, a daughter of Sargon of Akkad and high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur about 2300 BC, has been celebrated as the earliest known named author, but Assyriologists debate whether she actually composed the works attributed to her [Wikipedia on Enheduanna]
