place/uruk.title: Uruk
place/uruk.summary: Uruk was a Sumerian city in southern Mesopotamia and one of the first large cities in the world, at its peak around 3200 to 2900 BCE.
facts: It has yielded some of the earliest known writing, on clay tablets from the Eanna temple precinct.
By about 2900 BCE a wall about 9 kilometers long enclosed roughly 600 hectares (6 square kilometers), with an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 residents.
Uruk is the legendary city of Gilgamesh.
The modern site is called Warka, in Iraq.
place/uruk.context: Uruk is central to The Urban Revolution and Invention of Writing. See Sumerians.
place/uruk.observer: The Observer notes that the first large city was also the place of the first writing, and that both served administration by a temple institution.
questions: How large was Uruk's population?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Wall about 9 km (3100-2900 BCE); about 6 km2 and 50,000-80,000 residents about 2900 BCE [English Wikipedia]

place/valley-of-the-kings.title: Valley of the Kings
place/valley-of-the-kings.summary: The Valley of the Kings is a valley on the west bank of the Nile opposite Thebes, in Egypt, where pharaohs of the New Kingdom were buried in rock-cut tombs from about 1500 to 1070 BCE.
facts: The Valley of the Kings served for royal burials of the 18th to 20th Dynasties, from about 1500 BCE until about 1070 BCE, and holds more than 60 tombs cut into limestone hills.
The rulers chose hidden rock-cut tombs in place of the pyramids of earlier periods, such as those at Giza.
Most tombs were robbed in antiquity; records of trials of tomb robbers survive from the 20th Dynasty, and priests later moved royal mummies to hidden caches.

The workmen's village of Deir el-Medina yielded ration accounts and an account of a strike over unpaid rations, traditionally placed around the 25th year of Ramesses III (about 1170 BCE) though the precise year is not firmly fixed, often described as one of the earliest recorded labor strikes.
Howard Carter found the tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62) in November 1922, largely intact and holding thousands of objects.
UNESCO inscribed Ancient Thebes with its Necropolis, including the Valley of the Kings, in 1979.
place/valley-of-the-kings.context: The Valley of the Kings served the Ancient Egyptians of the New Kingdom, whose main temple was Karnak, and it replaced the pyramid tradition of the Giza Necropolis. It sits in the Bronze Age and the region Nile Valley, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief, Art and Ritual and Technology.
place/valley-of-the-kings.observer: The Observer notes that the move from monumental pyramids to hidden rock-cut tombs changed how rulers guarded their grief-rite investment: concealment replaced display, yet the tombs were still robbed, which suggests that no design made a store of wealth safe from the people who knew where it was. The strike at Deir el-Medina shows that the workforce building a ruler's afterlife was paid in rations and could act collectively when payment failed. The reading would weaken if the shift from pyramids proves to have been driven mainly by changes in belief and not by fear of robbery.
questions: Why did New Kingdom rulers abandon pyramids for hidden tombs?
How many people worked on the royal tombs, and how were they organized?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Royal burials in the Valley of the Kings spanned the Eighteenth to Twentieth Dynasties, from approximately 1539 BC to 1075 BC. [Wikipedia on Valley of the Kings]
2026-09-27: The Valley of the Kings is a wadi on the west bank of the Nile opposite Thebes (modern Luxor) and is known to contain 65 tombs and chambers. [Wikipedia on Valley of the Kings]
2026-09-27: Howard Carter discovered the tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62) in November 1922, the first royal tomb found in the valley that was still largely intact. [Wikipedia on Valley of the Kings]
2026-09-27: The site was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979 under the name Ancient Thebes with its Necropolis. [Wikipedia on Valley of the Kings]
2026-09-27: Tomb laborers of Deir el-Medina walked off the job over delayed grain rations in what may have been the first sit-down strike action in recorded history. [Wikipedia on Deir el-Medina]

place/varanasi.title: Varanasi
place/varanasi.summary: Varanasi, also called Benares or Kashi, is a city on the Ganges in Uttar Pradesh, India, continuously settled since about the 8th century BCE and the most important Hindu pilgrimage and cremation center.
facts: Varanasi lies on the left bank of the Ganges in Uttar Pradesh, and excavations at Rajghat show settlement from about the 8th century BCE.

Hindu tradition holds that dying at Varanasi and being cremated beside the Ganges gives release from the cycle of rebirth, so families bring their dead from across India to cremation sites such as Manikarnika, and more than 80 bathing and cremation steps (ghats) line the river.
The Buddha is traditionally said to have given his first sermon at Sarnath, near Varanasi, in about the 5th century BCE; Sarnath has an Ashokan pillar and Gupta-period sculpture.
Varanasi has been a center of Sanskrit learning, and Banaras Hindu University was founded in 1916; the city is also known for silk weaving.

The Kashi Vishwanath temple was destroyed and rebuilt several times, and the present temple dates from 1780; the adjacent Gyanvapi Mosque and the history of the site are the subject of continuing legal disputes.
Varanasi had about 1.2 million people at the 2011 census.
place/varanasi.context: Varanasi grew up on the Ganges River in the world of the Vedic Period, was linked with the Buddhist state of the Maurya Empire and the Gupta Empire through Sarnath, and later came under the Mughal Empire. It sits in the Iron Age and the region South Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief, Art and Ritual and Kinship and Society.
place/varanasi.observer: The Observer notes that Varanasi is a place where the grief-rite is the local institution: bodies from far away are brought to the riverbank because a meaning-engine teaches that death there brings release, and a supporting economy of priests, wood sellers and boatmen has formed around the practice. A Buddhist site, Hindu temples and a mosque within a few kilometers show several meaning-engines using one stretch of river, and the continuing dispute over one temple and mosque pair shows claim-lines still being drawn around old buildings. The reading would weaken if the cremation trade proves to be a small part of the city's economy compared with its other trades.
questions: How large was Varanasi in the 1st millennium BCE, and how did it compare with other Ganges cities?
How many cremations take place at Varanasi each year?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Varanasi lies on the left bank of the Ganges in the southeastern part of Uttar Pradesh, India, and the article calls it one of the world's oldest continually inhabited cities [Wikipedia on Varanasi]

2026-09-27: Excavations in 2014 turned up artefacts dating back to 800 BCE at Varanasi, and excavations at the nearby sites of Aktha and Ramnagar found artefacts dating back to 1800 BCE [Wikipedia on Varanasi]

2026-09-27: Varanasi has at least 84 ghats, of which Manikarnika and Harishchandra are the cremation ghats, and Kashi is listed among the seven cities known as givers of liberation (moksha) in Hindu tradition [Wikipedia on Varanasi]
2026-09-27: The 2011 census counted 1,212,610 people in the Varanasi municipal corporation and cantonment board area and 1,435,113 in the urban agglomeration [Wikipedia on Varanasi]

place/venice.title: Venice
place/venice.summary: Venice is a city on islands in a lagoon at the head of the Adriatic Sea in northeastern Italy, settled from about the 5th to 6th century CE and, as an independent republic until 1797, a leading maritime and trading power of the Mediterranean.
facts: Tradition dates Venice's founding on lagoon islands to 25 March 421, but no surviving records deal with it directly; the date_start of 500 is a round placeholder for settlement in the 5th to 6th centuries.

Nominally under Byzantine authority, Venice became self-governing under elected doges, dated by tradition from 697 and by historians from the early 8th century; about 810 the ducal seat moved to the Rialto.

In 1204 a Crusade fleet supplied by Venice under Doge Enrico Dandolo sacked Constantinople, and Venice took a large share of the Byzantine lands, including Crete; wars with the Ottoman Empire later cost it Negroponte (1470), Cyprus (1570 to 1573) and Crete (1669).

Venice opened a plague hospital on the island of Santa Maria di Nazareth in 1423, regarded as the first permanent lazaretto, and a second, Lazzaretto Nuovo, in 1468, and its isolation of arriving people and goods became an early model of quarantine.
In 1516 the Republic required its Jewish residents to live in an enclosed district called the Ghetto, whose name later spread to other cities.
The Great Council voted to end the Republic on 12 May 1797, as French forces approached; Austria received Venice under the Treaty of Campo Formio, and it joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1866.
UNESCO inscribed Venice and its Lagoon in 1987; the historic center's population fell from about 175,000 in the 1950s to under 50,000, and the MOSE flood barriers were first raised in October 2020.
place/venice.context: Venice was a partner and then a rival of Constantinople, took part in the Crusades, and lost ground to the Ottomans after the Fall of Constantinople in 1453. Its lazaretto system followed the Black Death, its painting and printing belong to the Renaissance, and the Republic ended during the Napoleonic Wars. Venice sits in the Medieval Period and the region Mediterranean Basin, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, War and Conflict and Art and Ritual.
place/venice.observer: The Observer notes that Venice, a state with almost no land of its own, made its story-glue from the sea: elected doges, councils that limited any one family, and a yearly ceremony in which the doge symbolically wed the Adriatic. A port lives on strangers and cargo, and the administration that built the lazaretto also enclosed the Jewish district in 1516, so a system built to manage risk also confined people, which the Observer records as a harm to those held. The reading would weaken if Venice's institutions differed little from those of other Italian maritime republics such as Genoa.
questions: How many people died in Venice in the plague outbreaks of 1348 and 1575 to 1577?
Can the lagoon city stay habitable and populated as sea level rises and the MOSE barriers age?

place/xingu-garden-cities.title: Xingu Garden Cities
place/xingu-garden-cities.summary: The Xingu garden cities are pre-Columbian settlements in the upper Xingu region of Brazil, dating from about 1200 to 1600 CE, whose plazas, roads, and ditches were mapped by the anthropologist Michael Heckenberger with the Kuikuro people.
facts: Researchers documented about 28 towns, villages, and hamlets, which may have supported up to about 50,000 people.
Larger towns had ditches about 3 meters deep and 10 meters wide, plazas up to 150 meters across, and roads aligned with the summer solstice.
Surrounding fields grew manioc, and earthen dams and ponds supported fish farming.
Population estimates are debated, and the descendants of the builders still live in the region.
place/xingu-garden-cities.context: See Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths. The settlements declined after 1500, as epidemics followed the Columbian Exchange.
place/xingu-garden-cities.observer: The Observer notes that the research was done together with the Kuikuro, whose descendants still live in the region. Living communities and archaeologists can inform each other.
questions: How many people lived in the Xingu network at its height?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: About 28 settlements, up to about 50,000 people, c. 1200-1600 CE; ditches about 3 m deep, plazas about 150 m [Scientific American on Xingu Garden Cities]

place/yellow-river.title: Yellow River
place/yellow-river.summary: The Yellow River (Huang He) is a river of northern China, about 5,460 kilometers long, whose loess-laden floodplain was a center of early farming and of the Shang and Zhou states, and whose floods and course changes have shaped Chinese history.
facts: The Yellow River rises in the Bayan Har Mountains of Qinghai and flows through northern China to the Bohai Sea.
Farming communities growing millet are documented in the Yellow River basin from about the 7th to 6th millennia BCE, and the Shang and Zhou states arose in its middle and lower reaches.

The Yellow River carries a heavy load of loess sediment from the Loess Plateau, which has raised its bed above the surrounding plain in the lower reaches and made dikes necessary; records list many breaches and several major changes of course.
From 1128 (some sources give 1194) until 1855 the river mostly ran south of the Shandong Peninsula into the Yellow Sea, until a breach around 1851 to 1855 returned it to a northern course.
A flood in 1887 is estimated to have killed between about 900,000 and 2 million people.

In 1938, during the Second Sino-Japanese War, Nationalist forces breached dikes at Huayuankou to slow the Japanese advance; several hundred thousand people died, with published estimates up to about 900,000, and millions were displaced.
place/yellow-river.context: The Yellow River is linked to The Agricultural Revolution in northern China, to the Shang Dynasty and the Han Dynasty as states that organized flood control, and to the Second Sino-Japanese War. It sits in the Neolithic and the region East Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life, War and Conflict and Technology.
place/yellow-river.observer: The Observer notes that a river that floods without warning helped tie authority to water control, and the traditional story of Yu the Great, who is said to have tamed the floods and founded the first dynasty, is a story-glue joining rule to engineering. The 1938 breach shows the same river used as sanctioned harm by a state against an invading army, with civilians as its main victims. The image of the Yellow River as the sole cradle of Chinese civilization is itself a story, since sites on the Yangtze and elsewhere also show early farming and state formation. The hypothesis that flood control drove state formation is contested, and specialists could weaken this reading by showing that other factors mattered more.
questions: How large was the death toll of the 1938 flood, and how many people were displaced?
How much did flood control contribute to early state formation compared with warfare and trade?

place/catalhoyuk.title: Çatalhöyük
place/catalhoyuk.summary: Çatalhöyük was a large Neolithic settlement in central Turkey, occupied from about 7100 to 5700 BCE, with houses packed together and entered from the roof.
facts: It held several thousand people at its height.
Walls bore paintings, and the dead were buried under house floors.
It had no streets; people walked across roofs.
It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.
place/catalhoyuk.context: Çatalhöyük is a site of the Neolithic. See Göbekli Tepe and The Settling and Its Bargain.
place/catalhoyuk.observer: The Observer notes a society living in one dense, continuous structure with few signs of rank. Early towns did not always show the hierarchy assumed for later cities.
